en: *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Scroll One:
The Seven Buddhas and the Indian Patriarchs; The Seven Buddhas and the Indian Patriarchs;
The Seven Buddhas.

Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha—among these fifteen patriarchs of India, only the first patriarch has collateral lineages recorded.
First Patriarch: Mahākāśyapa. Second Patriarch: Ānanda (with collateral lineage: Madhyāntika).
The Third Patriarch, Śaṇavāsa; the Fourth Patriarch, Upagupta; the Fifth Patriarch, Dīpamkara; the Sixth Patriarch, Micchaka;
the Seventh Patriarch, Vasumitra; the Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi;
the Ninth Patriarch, Puṇyamitra; the Tenth Patriarch, Pārśva; and the Eleventh Patriarch, Punayaśas.
The twelfth patriarch was the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa; the thirteenth patriarch was Kāpimora; the fourteenth patriarch was the Great Being Nāgārjuna.
Regarding the enumeration of the seven Buddhas: the seven Buddhas, as well as the ancient Buddhas, have appeared in the world.
Their succession extends infinitely;
it cannot be fully known or enumerated.
Therefore, it is said that in the present Bhadrakalpa, there are one thousand Tathāgatas.
Down to Śākyamuni,
only the seven Buddhas are recorded.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
The seven Buddhas, by the power of their diligence,
emit light that extinguishes the darkness;
each sits beneath his respective tree.
Within this, he attained perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of the seven Buddhas;
he is the Great Being Suṇhīta (Golden Flower) of the Golden Splendor.
While practicing the Way atop Mount Songshan,
he was moved by the vision of the Seven Buddhas leading before him and Vimalakīrti following behind;
this is the account of his current composition.
The lineage is severed from the seven Buddhas downward.
Regarding Vipaśyin Buddha—Vipaśyin Buddha, the nine hundred and ninety-eighth honored one of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*—the verse says:
The body is born from within the signless, just as various forms are produced by illusion;
the illusory person's mind and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, and both transgression and merit are empty, having no place of abiding.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste and the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was Bandhumat and his mother was Bandhumatī;
they resided in the city of Bandhumatī.
Sitting beneath a pāṭala tree,
he preached the Dharma in three assemblies,
delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people.
There were two who possessed the divine feet (ṛddhipāda): the first was named Khaṇḍa,
and the second was named Tiṣya.
The attendant was Aśoka.
His successor was Upagupta.
Regarding Śikhin Buddha—the nine hundred and ninety-ninth Tathāgata of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*—the verse says:
The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the commission of all evil karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam, and the mind is like the wind; they are produced by illusion, lacking roots and devoid of real nature.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was born into the Kṣatriya caste and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was named Mingxiang (Clear Signs) and his mother was named Guangyao (Radiant Splendor);
they resided in the city of Guangxiang (City of Radiant Signs).
Seated beneath a Pāṇḍuravimśa tree,
he preached the Dharma in three assemblies,
delivering two hundred and fifty thousand people.
There are two types of *ṛddhipāda*: first, *abhijñā*; second, *vaśitā*.
The attendant was Renxing;
his son was Wuliang.
The verse of the first of the thousand Buddhas of the Auspicious Kalpa (Bhadrakalpa), Vipaśyin Buddha, says:
Borrowing the four great elements to form a body, the mind is fundamentally without birth, arising only because of objects.
If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent; transgressions and blessings are like illusions—they arise and then perish.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
When the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste and the Kauṇḍinya clan.
His father was named Good Lamp;
his mother was named Renowned Virtue;
they resided in the city of Beyond Analogy.
Seated beneath a *śāla* tree,
he preached the Dharma in two assemblies,
delivering one hundred and thirty thousand people across the threshold of liberation.

There are two bases of supernormal power: first, the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration due to desire; second, the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration due to effort. (Note: The Chinese terms *fu you* and *yu duo mo* correspond to *chanda-samādhi* and *vīrya-samādhi*, respectively.)
His attendant was Śānta;
his son was Sujñāna.
Kṛkī Buddha, the first honored one currently appearing in the Bhadrakalpa, spoke these verses:
To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion.
To fully realize that the nature of both body and mind is empty—how could such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world;
he was of the Brahmin caste and the Kāśyapa clan.
His father was named Datta;
his mother was named Śākhā.
They resided in the city of Anavatapta.
Sitting beneath a śirīṣa tree,
he preached the Dharma in a single assembly,
delivering forty thousand people across.
There are two divine feet: first, Sani; second, Vīlu.
The attendant was Sujāta;
his son was Jinaśreṣṭha.
The verse concerning Krakucchanda Buddha, the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, says:
The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; If there were truly a knowing, there would be no Buddha apart from that knowing.
One who possesses wisdom can know that the nature of sin is empty, And remains serene, without fear of birth and death.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Brahmin caste Kāśyapa;
his father was Mahāguṇa.
The mother, Bhadraśrī,
resided in the city of Śuddhavatī and sat beneath an udumbara tree belonging to a brahmin.
In a single assembly, he preached the Dharma and delivered thirty thousand people.
His supernormal powers were of two kinds.
First, Śūrpāraka; second, Uttara;
with Ananda as his attendant.
The Disciple of the Teacher, Kāśyapa Buddha—the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa—spoke this verse:
"The nature of all sentient beings is pure; From the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished."
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world."
He was of the Brahmin caste,
of the Kāśyapa clan,
and his father was named Brahmadeva.
The mother, a mistress of wealth,
resided in the city of Vārāṇasī;
she sat beneath a nyagrodha tree.
He preached the Dharma in a single assembly,
delivering twenty thousand people;
he possessed two [kinds of] supernormal powers.
First, Tiṣya; second, Bharadvāja;
and the attendant was Kalyāṇamitra.
His son assembled the army.
Śākyamuni Buddha, the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa, was of the Kṣatriya caste;
his father was King Śuddhodana.
His mother was exceedingly pure and wondrous;
having attained the rank of the Stage of Rebirth, she was born in the Tuṣita Heaven,
known as the celestial being Śubhavati.
He is also named the Great Being Rakṣaprajñā;
he delivers the multitudes of devas and expounds the practices of the stage of succession to Buddhahood,
while also manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states:
When the Buddha was first born into the family of the Kṣatriyas,
he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Golden lotuses sprang up from the earth to spontaneously support his two feet;
he walked seven paces each toward the east, west, north, and south,
pointed his fingers at heaven and earth, and let out a lion’s roar.
Above, below, and in the four intermediate directions, there was none who could surpass me.
This was on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin, the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of Zhou.
It continued until the eighth day of the second month in the forty-second year.
At the age of nineteen, he desired to leave the household life.
He thought to himself,
"What further encounter shall I have?"
While wandering and observing at the four gates, he witnessed these four occurrences;
with feelings of both sorrow and joy arising in his mind, he reflected:
"This aging, illness, death, and ultimate end are truly to be weary of and renounced."
Then, at the hour of the rat during that night,
a celestial being named Śuddhāvāsa appeared through the window and, with palms joined, addressed the Prince, saying:
"The time for renunciation has arrived; you may depart.
Upon hearing this, the Prince felt joy arise in his heart and immediately leaped over the city wall and went away.
He practiced the path on Mount Dantaka.
Initially, at the abode of Ārāḍa Kālāma,
he studied the concentration of the sphere of nothingness for three years.
Realizing it was not [the way], he abandoned it.
He then went to the place of Udraka Rāmaputra and studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for three years.
Knowing them to be mistaken, he also abandoned them.
Furthermore, at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he joined with various non-Buddhist practitioners,
subsisting on hemp and wheat for six years.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"By means of being without mind, intention, or volitional activity, he completely subdues all non-Buddhists.
Having first tested them through heterodox methods and demonstrated various skillful means, he causes those with divergent views to reach Bodhi."
Therefore, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states:
"On the eighth day of the second month, at the time when the morning star appears,
the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood and is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
At that time he was thirty years of age;
it was the third year of King Mu’s reign, the year of Guiwei.
Subsequently, in the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), he...
For the sake of the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and expounded upon the fruits of the Path.
He taught the Dharma for forty-nine years while remaining in the world.
Later, he addressed his disciple Mahākāśyapa.
I entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, and the subtle, correct Dharma of the true mark that is signless.
You must protect and uphold it.
Furthermore, I command Ānanda as my successor to transmit and transform others, ensuring that it never be severed.
And he spoke in verse:
“The Dharma is originally the non-Dharma; The non-Dharma is also the Dharma.
Now, at the time of entrusting the non-Dharma, How has any dharma ever been a dharma?”
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses,
he further addressed Kāśyapa:
"I shall now transmit to you this saṃghāṭī robe woven with golden threads."
He transmitted it to the one in the position of succession,
saying, "Until the appearance of the Buddha Maitreya, do not let this decay.
Upon hearing these verses, Kāśyapa prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet and said:
Excellent, excellent!
I shall comply with your command,
out of reverent obedience to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly:
"I now suffer from back pain and wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
He immediately went to the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River,
where he lay down on his right side with his feet叠疊 (one upon the other) in profound stillness and tranquility.
Then, rising from the coffin, he preached the Dharma for his mother.
He specially manifested his two feet to transform Vakkula, and spoke this verse on impermanence:
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; They are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, [there is peace].
When it was said that "nirvāṇa is bliss," the disciples immediately vied with one another to cremate [the Buddha] with fragrant wood.
After the embers were extinguished, the golden coffin remained as it had been.
Thereupon, the great assembly praised the Buddha before him with these verses:
How could the fierce and blazing fires of the common world succeed in incinerating [the body]?
I pray that the Honored One’s fire of samādhi may cremate this golden-hued body.
At that time, the golden coffin rose from its seat to a height of seven tala trees.
Ascending and descending through the air, he manifested the Samādhi of Fire, and in an instant, ashes were produced.
Eight *hu* and four *dou* of śarīra were obtained;
this was on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, the *Renshen* year.
One thousand and seventeen years after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, the teaching reached the Central Plains;
this was precisely the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the year Wuchen.
This was the lineage of the Indian patriarchs.
His father was named Yinze (Drinking the Marsh) and his mother was named Xiangzhi (Fragrant Will). In the past, they were goldsmiths.
It skillfully clarifies the nature of gold, making it pliant and submissive.
The *Fofa zhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma Transmission) states:
"Once, in the distant past, after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha..."
The fourfold assembly erected a stūpa.
Within the stūpa, there was a slight flaw and damage upon the golden surface of the Buddha’s face.
At that time, a poor woman took a gold bead to a goldsmith and requested that he adorn the Buddha’s face with it.
Thereupon, they made a vow together,
wishing that the two of them might be husband and wife without marriage.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas their bodies were entirely golden in color.
Thereafter, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
When his celestial lifespan ended, he was born into a Brahmin family in the central kingdom of Magadha, named Kāśyapa.
This refers to the Honored One known as Kāśyapa;
he was so named because his complexion was golden.
Consequently, he resolved to seek renunciation, hoping to deliver all beings from the realms of existence.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣus. Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies.
He constantly praised me as the foremost among the assembly,
saying further:
"I entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye."
"You should propagate it so that it does not become extinct.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvāṇa..."
Kāśyapa was not present in the assembly.
The Buddha addressed the great disciples, saying,
"When Kāśyapa arrives, you should have him proclaim the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye."
At that time, Kāśyapa was in the Piṇḍava Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
beholding a supreme radiance, he immediately entered samādhi and,
with his purified divine eye, perceived the World-Honored One.
On the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River, he entered parinirvāṇa and addressed his disciples, saying:
"The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa."
"How swift it is! Having arrived between the twin trees, he wept with piteous longing.
The Buddha then manifested his two feet from within the golden coffin.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Buddha has already been cremated;
the adamantine relics are no longer our concern."
"We ought now to assemble the Dharma-eye so that it shall not be severed.
Then he spoke this verse:
"Disciples of the Tathāgata, do not yet enter nirvāṇa; those who have attained supernatural powers..."
When it was time to proceed to the council, those who had attained supernatural powers all assembled at the Piṇḍola Cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Ānanda was unable to enter the assembly because his outflows were not yet exhausted.
Subsequently, he realized the fruit of arhatship and thereby gained entry.
Kāśyapa then addressed the assembly, saying:
This bhikṣu Ānanda is of great learning and possesses great wisdom.
He has constantly followed the Tathāgata with pure brahmacarya.
Whatever Dharma he hears is like water being passed from one vessel to another, without any remainder.
"He whom the Buddha praised as foremost in intelligence should be requested to compile the Sūtra Piṭaka.
The great assembly remained silent.
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda,
"You should now proclaim the Eye of the Dharma.
Having heard these words, Ānanda accepted them with faith.
Observing the minds of the assembly,
he proclaimed these verses:
"O bhikṣus, even with all their retinues, those who are apart from the Buddha lack true adornment."
"Just as in the midst of the stars within the void there is no moon," he said.
Having spoken this verse,
he prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, ascended the Dharma seat, and spoke these words:
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling in a certain place, preaching a certain sutra and teaching.
[The assembly,] including humans and devas, paid homage and practiced accordingly.
At that time, Kāśyapa asked the bhikṣus:
"Is what Ānanda has said not erroneous?
They all replied,
"It is no different from what the World-Honored One has taught."
Kāśyapa then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The time for my life is not long;
I now entrust the True Dharma to you."
Guard it well. Listen to my verse:
"Every phenomenon is the primordial nature; there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon."
Having spoken the verse: "How can there be both dharma and non-dharma within a single dharma?
he then took up his saṃghāṭī robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
He waited for the descent of Maitreya;

this was the fifth year of King Xiaowang of the Zhou dynasty, the *bingchen* year. (The "fifth year" should be corrected to the "fourth year. From this point until the thirteenth patriarch, Kāpimora, the number of years contains errors; these are now all corrected according to the sexagenary cycle (*liu jia*) in the chronological tables of the *Shiji*.
He was of the Kṣatriya caste;
his father was King Droṇodana,
who was indeed the younger brother of the Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language it is Ānanda;
here it is translated as "Celebratory Joy" (Qingxi) or also as "Rejoicing" (Huanxi).
He was born on the night the Tathāgata attained enlightenment;
he was widely learned, profoundly erudite, and possessed unimpeded wisdom.
The World-Honored One regarded him as the foremost among those who possess dhāraṇī.
I have previously praised them;
moreover, they possess great merit from past lives and uphold the treasury of the Dharma like water being passed from one vessel to another.
The Buddha then appointed him as his attendant.
Later, King Ajātaśatru addressed him, saying:
"O Virtuous One!"
The Tathāgata and the two honored and preeminent teachers, Kāśyapa and Śāriputra, have both already entered parinirvāṇa;
because of my many karmic hindrances, I was unable to behold them all,
O virtuous one.
"At the time of my parinirvāṇa, I wish for you to grant me leave.
Ānanda consented to this.
Later, he thought to himself:
My body is fragile and precarious, like a mass of foam;
how much more so now that it is aged and decrepit—how could it endure for long?
Furthermore, he reflected:
"King Ajātaśatru has an agreement with me;
therefore, I have come to the royal palace to bid him farewell before entering nirvana."
The gatekeeper said, "The King is sleeping; he must not be disturbed. Ānanda said:
"I shall explain this to you when Your Majesty has awakened.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw in a dream a precious parasol,
adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded and gazed upon by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis.
Suddenly, a violent wind and rain arrived, blowing and breaking its handle;
the precious jewels and necklaces all fell to the ground,
which left his heart deeply struck with wonder.
Upon waking,
the gatekeeper reported the aforementioned matter in full; having heard these words,
the King wailed aloud with such grief that his lamentation moved both heaven and earth.
He immediately arrived at the city of Vaiśālī and saw Ānanda sitting cross-legged in the middle of the stream of the Gaṅgā River.
The king then paid homage and spoke this verse:
I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms, who has left me behind to reach this place;
for the time being, rely upon the power of your compassionate vow and do not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, King Vaiśālī was also by the riverbank.
Again, he spoke in verse:
"Venerable One, why do you return so swiftly to the field of nirvana?
We pray that you remain for a brief moment to accept our offerings."
At that time, Ānanda, seeing the two kings both coming to offer their entreaties, spoke this verse:
"O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not give way to bitter sorrow or longing."

"Nirvāṇa is my purity" (the original text reads "quiescence," which has been changed to this single character based on the *Baolin zhuan* and the *Zhengzong ji*); because it is free from all existence, Ānanda thought again:
If I were to enter parinirvāṇa while favoring one particular kingdom,
it would lead to strife and contention among the various nations; such a thing is impossible.
One should deliver all sentient beings through equanimity;
thus, while in the middle of the river of permanence, he was about to enter nirvana.
At that time, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Within the Snowy Mountains, there were five hundred rishis who,
beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air to arrive.
They prostrated at Ānanda’s feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and addressed him, saying:
"I shall bear witness to the Buddha-dharma before you, Venerable One.
We pray that you will extend great compassion and deliver us.
Ānanda accepted the request in silence.
He immediately transformed the Ganges River entirely into golden ground and expounded various great Dharmas for that assembly of sages.
Ānanda thought again:
"The disciples whom I have previously delivered and liberated should now assemble.
In a brief moment, five hundred arhats descended from the sky and,
for the sake of the various seers, granted them the going forth and full ordination.
Among that assembly of sages were two arhats:
the first was named Śāṇakavāsin,
and the second was named Madhyandina.
Ānanda, knowing that he was a vessel for the Dharma,
told him: "In the past,
the Tathāgata entrusted the Great Eye of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa."
Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption and entrusted it to me;
I am now about to pass away, so that I may transmit it to you. You must receive my teaching.
Listen now to these verses:
The Dharma originally entrusted is existent; Having been entrusted, it is said to be non-existent.
Each must awaken for themselves; Upon awakening, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Having completed the entrustment of the Dharma-eye treasury to Ānanda,
he leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations.
He entered the *vāyu-vikrīḍita-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Swift Play of Wind) and divided his body into four parts.
One portion was offered to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
one portion was offered to the Palace of the Sāgara Dragon King;

and one portion was offered to Vaiśālī—where the original text reads "Vaiśālī Dragon King," but following the *Bǎolín zhuàn* and the *Zhèngzōng jì*, the characters for "Dragon King" have been removed.
One portion was presented to King Ajātaśatru, and each had a precious stūpa constructed to enshrine it and offer worship.
This was in the twelfth year of King Li, the guisi year; however, it should be calculated as the tenth year.
Regarding the Third Patriarch, Śaṇavāsa: the *Zhengzongji* states that the Sanskrit name Śaṇavāsa translates into Chinese as "Naturally Clothed."
This is because at the time of his birth, he already possessed robes.
Hong Juefan’s *Zhilin* states that this means the *saṃghāṭī* robe was identical to that of Yunyan.
Yet the *Chuan deng lu* states that his name was Ziranfu;
he was a native of the country of Mathurā in the Western Regions, whose personal name is unknown.
He was also called Śīlabhadra and belonged to the Viśākha clan.
His father was Vana-vijaya and his mother was Kausheya;
he was born after being in the womb for six years.
In Sanskrit it is called *śaṇakha*;
here it is translated as "naturally grown garment.
This refers to the name of a nine-branched, exquisite herb found in the Western Regions.
If an Arhat or noble being is born, these grasses grow in clean and pure places;
when Andhaka was born, these auspicious grasses appeared in response.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata traveled to teach and transform beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā.
Seeing a green forest with lush branches and leaves,
he said to Ānanda,
"The name of this forest is Uruvilvā."
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
there will be a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma in this place."
One hundred years later, Guo Dan was born;
he left the household life to realize the Way and received the Dharma-eye of the Venerable Ānanda.
He converted sentient beings and settled in this grove;
he subdued the two fire-dragons (nāgas) so they would submit to the Buddha's teachings.
Because the dragons offered him their land, he established the Brahma Palace (Brahmavihāra).
After the Venerable One had long been engaged in his work for the sake of beings, he thought of entrusting the True Dharma [to a successor].
He then found Upagupta in the kingdom of Mathurā and took him as his attendant.
Consequently, he asked Upagupta:
"How old are you? He replied,
"I am seventeen years old."
The Master said,
"Are the seventeen elements of your body also seventeen?
He replied:
The Master’s hair has turned white.
Is it the hair that has turned white,
or is it the mind?
The Master said,
"I am merely white-haired;
it is not that my mind is white."
Kumāralāta said:
"My body is seventeen;
it is not that my nature is seventeen."
Huixiu recognized that he was a vessel for the Dharma;
three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him.
He then told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the unsurpassed treasury of the Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa."
It has been transmitted from one to another until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; do not let it be interrupted.
Receive my teaching.
Listen to my verse:
"There is no mind and there is no dharma. When this mind-dharma is spoken, that dharma is not the mind-dharma. Having finished speaking the verse:
He then withdrew into the White Elephant Mountain in the southern region of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he beheld his disciple Guptaka,
who had a following of five hundred disciples that were frequently characterized by indolence and arrogance.
The Venerable One then went to that place and,
manifesting the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi (*nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi*),
subdued him and spoke this verse:
"Thoroughly penetrating that which is neither this nor that, The Most Holy One has neither long nor short.
Abandon your thoughts of contempt, And you shall swiftly attain arhatship.

One day, while traveling on the road to Huangmei County,

The Master asked him:

The Master asked,

During the Wude era, I traveled to Mount Lu.

The Master submitted a memorial declining the invitation three times in succession.

For the fourth time, the king commanded his messenger, saying:
"If he does not rise, then bring his head here."
The envoy arrived at the mountain to deliver the imperial decree.
The Master then extended his neck toward the blade with an expression of solemn composure.
The envoy was struck by this marvel and returned to report the circumstances to the throne.
The Emperor sighed with admiration and bestowed upon him precious silks to fulfill his aspirations.
This reached as far as the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month of the Xinhai year of the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong.
Suddenly, he issued this admonition to his disciples:
"All dharmas are entirely liberated.
Each of you should protect and mind yourselves, spreading this teaching to future generations."

On the eighth day of the fourth month the following year, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord without cause.
The ritual appearance was as if he were still alive.

From his parinirvāṇa until the first year of the Jingtai era of the Great Song (the Jiachen year), there were exactly three hundred and fifty-six years—though it should be stated as three hundred and fifty-four years.
As for the thirty-second patriarch, Master Hongren: he was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.
His surname was Zhou.
From birth, he was precocious and intelligent.
While playing as a child, he encountered a wise man.
He sighed and said,
"This son lacks seven marks and does not equal the Tathāgata.
Later, upon meeting the Great Master Xìn, he will obtain the Dharma succession and transform [others]."
During the Xianheng era at Mount Pótóu, there was a lay practitioner (jūshì) surnamed Lú and named Huínéng.
He came from Qīnzhōu— where the New and Old editions erroneously write the character “Qiāo”— to pay his respects to the Master.
The questioner asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "From Lingnan.
The Master asked, "What do you require?"
[Qiu] said, "I only seek to become a Buddha.
The Master said,
"People south of the ridge have no Buddha-nature."
"If one were to attain Buddhahood," [the monk] said,
"would it mean that humans possess both northern and southern Buddha-natures?
The Master knew he was an extraordinary person.
He then rebuked him, saying,
"Go and stay in the stable.
Nanda prostrated at his feet and withdrew.
He then entered the millhouse and took up manual labor among the pestles and mortars,
working day and night without rest for eight months.
The Master knew that the time for transmission had arrived.
He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it cannot be grasped by merely memorizing my words and taking them as one's own burden.
Each of you should, according to your own inclination, compose a verse."
If his words and intentions were in perfect accord,
then both the robes and the Dharma would be transmitted to him.
At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.
As for the Venerable Shenxiu,
his learning encompassed both Buddhist and non-Buddhist traditions, and he was revered by all;
everyone together praised him, saying:
"If it were not for one as venerable and eminent as you, who would dare to accept this?
Shenxiu has privately heard the acclaim of the multitude and, without further reflection,
has inscribed a verse upon the wall of the corridor, saying:"
"The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror-stand.
At all times diligently wipe it clean; Do not allow dust to collect.
The Master, while walking for exercise, suddenly saw this verse.
Knowing that this was composed by Shenxiu,
he then praised it, saying:
"Those of future generations who practice according to this shall also attain supreme fruits."
Originally, he had intended for the recluse Lu Zhen to paint the *Lengqie* transformation scenes on the wall;
however, upon seeing the inscribed verses on it,
he desisted from painting and instead ordered everyone to recite them.
While at the mortar-house, he suddenly heard someone reciting a verse.
He then asked his fellow student,
"What chapter or passage is this?"
A fellow student said,
"The Master does not know that you are seeking a Dharma heir,
which is why he has ordered each of you to compose a verse expressing your state of mind."
This was recounted by the Venerable Xiu, whom the Master deeply praised and commended.
He remarked, "He will surely be the one to whom the Dharma is entrusted and the robe transmitted. Thus it was said.
"What is that verse? His fellow student recited it for him,
and he was able to repeat it after a long time.
"It is beautiful indeed,
yet it is not yet fully realized.
His fellow students rebuked him, saying:
"What does a common person know? Do not utter such mad words.
Neng said, "Do you not believe me?"
"I wish for you to harmonize with me using a single verse.
His fellow student did not answer, but merely looked at him and smiled.
[The Master] waited until nightfall, then secretly informed a young boy, who led him down to the corridor.
He was able to hold a candle himself and had the youth write a verse beside the "Elegant Verses" (Xiùjì), which said:
Enlightenment is fundamentally not a tree; The mirror of the mind is likewise not a stand.
"Originally there was not a single thing; why should one bother to sweep away dust?
When the Great Master saw this verse later, he said, "Who wrote this? They have not yet seen their nature."
When the assembly heard the Master’s words, they paid them no heed.
When night fell, he secretly sent someone from the millhouse to summon a capable practitioner to his room, saying:

Guard them well yourself, and do not allow them to be severed.

"What more need be asked?
He asked again, "Regarding the rules for robes, who is it that receives them?

Regarding the collateral lineages descending from the Thirty-first Patriarch, Grand Master Daoxin: the first generation descendant in the sixth lineage of the Ancestral Patriarchs at Mount Niutou in Jinling was Chan Master Farong.
As for this first-generation Chan Master Farong:
He was a native of Yanling in Runzhou and surnamed Wei. At the age of nineteen,
his mastery of the Confucian classics and histories was thorough.
Having searched through the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and attained a clear understanding of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
he suddenly sighed one day, saying:
"The classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate teaching."
Prajñā and right contemplation are the vessel for transcending the world.
He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he shaved his head under a master.
Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou.
There was the marvel of a hundred birds carrying flowers in their beaks.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric portents from afar and knew that there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain.
He then personally went to inquire of the temple monks, asking,
"Is there any practitioner of the Way here?
They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, which one is not a practitioner of the Way?"
The Patriarch said,
"Which one here is a man of the Way?
The monk had no reply.
Another monk said,
"About ten li from here in the mountains there is one named Lanrong;
he does not rise when seeing people, nor does he join his palms."
"Perhaps you are a man of the Way.
The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, looking about with no concern whatsoever.
The Patriarch asked,
"What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am contemplating the mind."
The Patriarch said,
"Observe what this person is and what this mind is.
The Master had no reply and simply rose to pay his respects.
The Master asked,
"Virtuous One, where do you dwell in seclusion?

Once, a monk named Jizong from Huayan Monastery asked,
"What is the meaning of 'seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood'?
The Master said:
The nature of purity is inherently tranquil and free from movement;
it does not belong to existence or non-existence, purity or impurity, length or shortness, nor to grasping or rejecting. Its essence is naturally detached and serene.
To perceive clearly in this manner is called seeing one's nature.
Nature is itself Buddha, and Buddha is itself nature;
therefore it is said that "seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood.
It is asked: since nature is pure and does not belong to existence or non-existence, how can this be?
"For what reason is there seeing?
The Master said,
"Seeing is the absence of anything seen."
[The student] asked: "If there is nothing seen, by what cause could there be further seeing?
The Master said: "Even the place of seeing is non-existent.
[The student] asked: "When it is seen in this way, whose seeing is it?"
The Master said,
"There is no one who can see it.
[The student] asked, "What is the ultimate principle of this?"
The Master said,
"Do you know? If you falsely reckon it as existing, then it exists."
The existence of subject and object is what constitutes delusion;
following one's perceptions to give rise to conceptual understanding leads one to fall into birth and death.
For one who sees with clarity, it is not so.
Throughout the entire day one sees that which has never been seen;
though one seeks the locus of seeing, its essential characteristics cannot be apprehended,
for both subject and object are utterly transcended.
This is called "seeing one's nature.
[The student] asked, "Does this nature pervade all places?
The Master said:
"There is nowhere it does not pervade.
[The questioner] asked, "Do ordinary people possess it?
The Master said:
It was stated above that there is nowhere it does not pervade;
how could ordinary beings not possess it?
[The questioner asks: For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death?
Yet ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering;
how could it ever be universal?
The Master said:
Ordinary beings, within the nature of purity, conceive of subject and object; thus they fall into birth and death.
The Buddhas and great beings, however, well know that within the nature of purity there belongs neither to existence nor to non-existence.
Thus, neither the subject nor the object can be established.
It is said: "If one speaks in this manner, there are those who understand and those who do not."
The Master said,
"If even 'understanding' cannot be apprehended,
how could there be a person who understands?"
[The questioner] asked, "What is the ultimate principle like?
The Master said,
"I shall speak of it in its essentials."
You should immediately reflect that within the nature of purity there are neither ordinary beings nor sages,
nor are there those who have realized it and those who have not.
Ordinary people and sages—both are merely names.
If one generates understanding by following these names, one falls into birth and death;
if one knows that these provisional names are not real, [one is liberated].
Thus, there is nothing that can be designated by a name.
It is further said:
"This is the ultimate point of finality."
To claim, "I can comprehend that while others cannot," is a great illness.
To perceive the existence of purity and defilement, or ordinary beings and sages, is likewise a great illness.
To form an understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages belongs to the category of denying cause and effect.
To perceive that there is a pure nature in which one may dwell is a great delusion;
to understand it as a state of non-dwelling is likewise a great delusion.
Nevertheless, within the nature of purity, there is no movement.
Possessing the application of indestructible skillful means,
as well as giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion—
wherever such [qualities] are aroused.
This is precisely the nature of total purity;
it may be called "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
The successor of the lineage leaped for joy.

There are those who shift [their views] according to direction; when they shift their direction, they claim that the principle remains without deviation.
If there is no deviation, then the contemplation of the essential meaning cannot differ.
The principle of non-differentiation is the *li* (principle);
the principle of non-discrepancy is the *zong* (tenet).
While the principle is one, the two—names and words—are used to clarify its manifestation; they are merely its playful extensions.
Tenth, regarding "Miraculously Accordance with the Profound Source":
Now, a practitioner who has awakened to the mind would never cling to the contemplation while remaining deluded about its ultimate purpose.
How could one who has attained the teaching stagnate in words and be deluded regarding the principle?
When the principle is clarified, the path of language is severed.
How can words discuss it?
When the ultimate meaning is realized, the sphere of mental activity ceases.
How can contemplation conceive of it?
That which cannot be conceived by mind or expressed in words may be called a wondrous resonance with the center of the universe.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Tianxian era, the Master sat peacefully and manifested his passing.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he was interred in a stupa on the southern slope of West Mountain.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Wuxiang (Master of Non-Form),
and his stupa was named Jingguang (Pure Light).
During the Chunhua era of the Song dynasty, Emperor Taizong issued an imperial decree for the local prefecture to reconstruct the grotto and stupa.
As for Chan Master Benjing of Mount Sikong, he was a native of Jangzhou.
His surname was Zhang.
In his youth, he donned the black robes at the monastery of Caoxi and received a prediction of enlightenment.
He was subsequently enrolled at Wuxiang Monastery on Mount Sīkong.
In the third year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, Emperor Xuānzōng dispatched the palace messenger Yáng Guāngtíng to enter the mountains to gather *chángchūn* (evergreen) vines.
He subsequently constructed a hall for the Master and paid his respects, inquiring:
"Your disciple has admired you for this long."
"I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will briefly grant me an instruction.
The Master said,
"The eminent scholars of the Chan school throughout the land have all assembled here in the capital."
"It would be sufficient for you, Celestial Messenger, to return to court to seek a definitive resolution.
As for me, a poor monk, I dwell by the mountains and beside the waters with no concerns in my mind.
Guangting prostrated himself in tears.
The Master said,
"Cease your prostrations to this poor monk.
Do you, messenger from heaven, seek the Buddha or inquire about the Way?"
The disciple said, "My wisdom and understanding are clouded and dim;
I have not yet discerned what the relationship between the Buddha and the Way is like.
The Master said:
If you wish to seek the Buddha, the very mind is the Buddha;
if you wish to realize the Way, the absence of mind is the Way.
[The questioner] asked: "In what sense is the very mind the Buddha?"
The Master said:
"The Buddha is realized through the mind, and the mind is manifested by means of the Buddha.
If one realizes the mindless state, even the Buddha does not exist."
He asked, "What is meant by 'no-mind is the Way'?
The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally without mind; no-mind is called the Way."
"If one realizes there is no mind, then no-mind is itself the Way.
Guangting prostrated himself and accepted this with faith. Having returned to the palace, he reported these words to the Emperor.
Wang Guangting reported in detail all that he had encountered in the mountains to the Emperor.
An imperial edict was immediately issued summoning the Master;
on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, he arrived in the capital and was commanded to reside at Bailian Pavilion.

In the first month of the following year, on the fifteenth day, he summoned eminent monks and great scholars from the two monastic districts to attend the Inner Sanctuary (Nei Daochang) with the Master to expound upon Buddhist principles.
At that time, there was a Chan Master named Yuan.
Raising his voice, he said to the Master,
"Now that we are before His Majesty to examine our respective tenets,
we ought to question and answer directly without resorting to elaborate rhetoric."
"According to what the Zen Master perceives, what constitutes the Way?
The Master replied,
"A mind free of intention is the Way."
Dyuan said: "The Way arises because of the mind.
How can you say that no-mind is the Way?"
The Master said:
"The Way is fundamentally nameless; it is because of the mind that the Way is named.
If the name 'mind' were not real, the Way would not be so either."
If the mind is fundamentally non-existent, what path can it rely upon to establish itself?
Both are empty and false, being nothing more than provisional names. Yuan said:
The Zen Master asked, "Do you see that body and mind are the Way?
The Master replied,
"The body and mind of this mountain monk have been the Way from the very beginning."
He said: "Previously you stated that being without mind is the Way;
now you say that body and mind are fundamentally the Way.
Are these not contradictory?"
The Master said:
"No-mind is the Way; when the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent.
Because mind and the Way are one and the same, it is said that no-mind is the Way."
Body and mind are originally the Way;
the Way is also originally body and mind.
Since body and mind are fundamentally empty, so too is the Way.
"The Way also reaches its source in non-existence.
Master Guan remarked, "This master's physical frame is quite small,
yet he understands this principle."
The Master said,
"Virtuous One,
you see only the appearance of this mountain monk."
The mountain monk has no marks;
that which you see, O Venerable One, is the seeing of marks.
As the Sūtra says:
All marks whatsoever are empty and false.
If one perceives that all marks are no-marks,
one immediately awakens to the Way.
"If one takes marks as real, one will not be able to awaken to the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas.
[The student] said, "I now request that the Meditation Master explain the markless upon the basis of marks.
The Master said:
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"The four great elements have no master, and the body likewise has no self.
To be free from the view of 'mine' is to be in accord with the Way."
"Venerable Sir,
if one considers the four great elements as having a master who is the self,
and if one possesses such a view of self, one will not be able to realize the Way even at the end of an eon."
Upon hearing these words, Master Yuan Gong turned pale with alarm; he hesitated for a moment and withdrew from his seat.
The Master had a verse that said:
"The four elements have no master and are like water; Meeting curves and encountering straightness, they know neither self nor other."
Neither pure nor impure places give rise to the mind; When obstructed or flowing, how could there ever be two intentions?
Contacting objects is merely like water having no mind; Acting freely and unrestrained in the world—what matters could there be?
Furthermore, it says:
As it is with one of the four great elements, so it is with the other three.
If one clearly realizes that the four great elements have no master,
one immediately awakens to the absence of mind.
If one realizes the absence of mind, one naturally accords with the Way.
Furthermore, there was a Chan Master named Zhiming who asked:
If it is said that being without mind is the Way,
then tiles and pebbles, which are also without mind, should likewise be the Way.
Furthermore, it is said:
The body and mind are fundamentally the Way.
Since the four modes of birth and the ten classes of beings all possess body and mind, they too should be the Way.
The Master said:
Venerable sir, if you form the conceptual understanding of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
it is far removed from the Way;
you are merely one who seeks seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
This is not for those who seek the Way.
As the Sūtra says:
"There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
If the six sense organs themselves lack seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, upon what could they possibly be established?
When one exhaustively investigates their origin and finds nothing, where can the mind abide?
How could it not be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles?
Zhiming closed his mouth and withdrew.
The Master further spoke a verse, saying:
"In seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing there is no obstruction; In sounds, scents, tastes, and touches, one is always in samādhi."
Like a bird flying through the air, simply so it flies—without grasping or rejecting, without hatred or love.
If you can understand that in its proper place there is fundamentally no mind, only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, there was a Chan Master named Zhen.
Question: Since the Way is without mind, does the Buddha have a mind?
Are the Buddha and the Way one or two?
The Master said,
"Neither one nor different.
[The monk] asked, "The Buddha delivers sentient beings because they possess a mind."
The Way does not save beings because it is without mind;
it saves some while not saving others—
how can there be no duality?
The Master said:
"If you say that while the Buddha delivers sentient beings, the Way has no one to deliver,
this is for you, Great Virtue, to have falsely given rise to dualistic views."
As for me, a mountain monk, it is not so.
"Buddha" is a hollow name and the "Way" is falsely established;
both are unreal and are entirely mere provisional designations.
Within a single conventional designation, how can one distinguish two?
It is asked:
"The Buddha and the Way are both derived from these conventional designations."
When a name is established,
who is it that establishes it?
If there is one who establishes it, how can you say it does not exist?
The Master said:
"Buddha and the Way are established based on the mind;
yet when one investigates to the ultimate the mind that establishes them, that mind is also non-existent."
Since the mind is non-existent, one realizes that both are unreal;
knowing them to be like dreams and illusions, one realizes they are fundamentally empty.
Thus, the two names "Buddha" and "Path" are merely established by force.
This is the view and understanding of those of the Two Vehicles.
The Master, however, teaches that there is neither cultivation nor action.
The verse says:
If one sees the path, then one cultivates the path; if one does not see it, what is there to cultivate?
The nature of the path is like space—what can space cultivate?
To look everywhere for one who cultivates the path is like beating out fire to seek a bubble.
Just observe the puppet show: when the string snaps, everything stops at once.
Furthermore, there was the Chan Master Fakong, who asked:
If both the Buddha and the Way are merely provisional names,
then the twelve divisions of the teachings must also be unreal. Why,
then, have all the venerable masters of the past spoken of "cultivating the Way"?
The Master said,
"Virtuous One, you have misunderstood the meaning of the scriptures.
The Way is fundamentally without cultivation, yet you, Virtuous One, insist upon cultivating it."
The Way is fundamentally without action, yet the great virtuous ones insist on acting;
the Way is fundamentally without affairs, yet they insist on creating many affairs;
the Way is fundamentally without knowledge, yet within it they insist on knowing.
Such a view is contrary to the Way.
The venerable masters of old would not have acted thus;
it is simply that you, Great Virtue, do not understand.
Please reflect upon this.
The Master further spoke in verse:
"The essence of the Way is fundamentally without cultivation; Without cultivating, one naturally accords with the Way."
If one gives rise to the mind of practicing the Way, this person will not realize the Way;
they abandon the single true nature and instead enter into a state of bustling confusion.
Even if they suddenly encounter a practitioner of the Way, they must at all costs not speak of it.
Furthermore, there was Master An who asked:
"Since the Way is but a provisional name, the Buddha is said to be falsely established."
The twelve divisions of the teachings are likewise for the purpose of guiding beings and delivering them from suffering.
Since all things are illusory, what can be considered real?
The Master said:
Because there is delusion, one contrasts the real with the delusory;
yet when one investigates the nature of delusion, it is fundamentally empty,
for how could the real ever have existed?
Thus we know that both truth and falsehood are merely provisional names;
these two phenomena, as mutual antidotes, possess no substantial reality.
When their fundamental source is investigated, all are entirely empty.
It is said: Since it has been stated that all things are illusory,
and illusion is identical to reality,
there is no distinction between reality and illusion.
"What thing is it? The Master said,
"If you ask what thing it is,"
Nothing whatsoever is false.
As the Sūtra says:
"There is nothing similar and no analogy."
"The path of language is cut off like a bird flying through the sky.
Master An was filled with shame and submission, not knowing what to do.
The Master further spoke a verse, saying:
Pushing to the truth, the truth has no marks; Exhausting the delusion, the delusion has no form.
Turning back to observe and exhaust the mind, One knows that the mind is also a provisional name.
Realizing the Way is likewise so; In the end, there is only peace.
Furthermore, there was a Chan Master named Daxing who asked:
"Chan is most subtle and most profound."
When both truth and falsehood are extinguished, both the Buddha and the Way perish;
the nature of cultivation is emptiness, and names and forms are unreal.
The world is like an illusion; all are but provisional designations.
When forming this understanding, one must not sever the two roots of good and evil within sentient beings.
The Master said:
"The two roots of good and evil both arise from the mind."
If the mind, when investigated to its limit, possessed a root, it would not be empty.
Since the mind, upon analysis, has no root, by what cause could it be established?
As the Sūtra says:
Wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are transformed and produced from the mind;
the conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma are fundamentally without reality.
Furthermore, the Master spoke a verse:
Since goodness arises from the mind, how could evil be separate from it?
If good and evil are external conditions, they do not truly exist within the mind.
Where would one cast away evil? Who would there be to guard the taking up of goodness?
Alas for those of dualistic views, who run hither and thither, clinging to both ends!
If one awakens to the fact that the mind is fundamentally non-existent, only then will one repent of former faults.
Furthermore, there was a close minister.
Question: From where does this body come?
After a hundred years, where does it return?
The Master said:
"When a person is dreaming, from where do they come?
When they wake up, to where do they go?"
It is said: At the time of dreaming, one cannot say it is non-existent;
once awakened, one cannot say it is existent.
Although there is this coming and going of existence and non-existence, there is no locus for them.
The Master said,
"This body of mine is also like a dream.
He further spoke a verse:
Viewing life as being like a dream—within the dream, there is indeed clamor;
suddenly awakening, all affairs cease. It is just like realizing it while still asleep.
The wise understand the dream; the deluded believe in the dream’s clamor.
Dreams and reality are as two different things; once awakened, there is no awakening other than that [awakening].
Wealth and honor and poverty and lowliness are likewise no different. Furthermore, there is no other path.
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Upper Yuan era, he passed into stillness.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Enlightenment Chan Master (Daxiao Chanshi). As for Chan Master Xuance of Wuzhou, he was a native of Jinhua in Wuzhou.
Having left home to travel as a wandering monk, he arrived at Heshuo.
There was a Chan Master named Huángzhì who once visited the Fifth Patriarch at Huangméi.
He lived in a hermitage for twenty years, considering himself to be in the state of right reception (*samyaksamādhi*).
The Master knew that Huáng’s realization was not yet authentic;
he went to him and asked,
"What are you doing sitting here?"
Huang said, "I have entered meditative absorption.
The Master said,
"You say you have entered meditative absorption."
Does it possess a mind, or is it without a mind?
If it possessed a mind, then all classes of wriggling creatures should be able to attain meditative concentration.
If it were without a mind, then all varieties of grasses and trees would likewise be capable of attaining meditative concentration.
He said, "When I am correctly entering meditative absorption,
I do not perceive a mind of either existence or non-existence.
The Master said:
Since one no longer perceives a mind of existence or non-existence,
this is constant samādhi;
how could there be entering or exiting?
"If there is coming and going, it is not the Great Samādhi.
Huang remained silent for a long while,
then asked the Master, "Whom do you follow as your teacher?"
The Master said,
"My teacher was the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.
[The questioner] asked, "What did the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration?"
The Master said: "My teacher said:
'Now, the wondrous, profound, and perfectly tranquil essence and its function are as such (as they truly are).'"
The five aggregates are fundamentally empty and the six sense objects do not exist.
There is no emerging and no entering; neither fixed nor disordered.
The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is a tranquil stillness that transcends all dwelling in dhyāna.
"The nature of dhyāna is non-arising; it is free from the conceptualization of dhyāna.
The mind is like empty space, yet it possesses no measure of empty space.
When Huáng heard this teaching, [he was moved].
He then traveled to Caoxi to request a resolution of his doubts and obscurations;
as the Patriarch’s intent and the Master’s realization were in profound accord,
Huáng finally attained awakening.
The Master later returned to Jinhua,
where he extensively opened his Dharma seat.
As for Chan Master Letao of Caoxi, he was a native of Jizhou.
His surname was Zhang.
He left the household life under the Sixth Patriarch and never departed from his side.
When the Patriarch entered nirvana, [Nanyue] became the master of his robe-stupa.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong heard of his virtuous reputation and issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital.
The Master declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.
In the first year of the Shangyuan era, Emperor Suzong dispatched an envoy to retrieve the Dharma robes for worship within the palace.
He subsequently issued an edict commanding the Master to enter the capital with the robes,
but the Master declined on the grounds of illness.
He passed away at his home mountain at the age of ninety-five. By imperial decree,
he was posthumously bestowed the title of Chan Master Daxiao.
National Teacher Huizhong of Guangzhai Monastery in the Western Capital was a native of Zhuji in Yuezhou.
His secular surname was Ran.
Having received the Mind-Seal (cittamudrā) for himself, he resided at Dangzigou in Baiyashan, Nanyang.
For more than forty years, he did not descend from the mountain gate.
His practice of the Way became renowned throughout the imperial capital.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial messenger, Sun Chaojin,
was dispatched with an edict to summon him to the capital,
where he was received with the honors due to a teacher.
Initially, he resided at the Xichanyuan (Western Chan Monastery) of Qianfu Temple.
When Emperor Daizong ascended the throne, he was again invited to stay at the Guangzhai Vihāra,
where he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners for sixteen years.
At that time, there was the Tripitaka Master Daili from Western Heaven who arrived at the capital and claimed to have attained the wisdom-eye of telepathy.
The Emperor issued an edict ordering him to undergo a trial with the National Preceptor.
As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Preceptor, he prostrated himself and stood to his right.
The Preceptor asked:
"Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?
He replied, "I dare not say so."
The Master said,
"Tell me, where am I, this old monk, right now?
He replied, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation."
"How can you go off to Xichuan to watch the boat races?
The Master asked again,
"Tell me, where am I right now?"
[The monk] said, "The Master is the teacher of an entire nation.
How can you be here on Tianjin Bridge watching monkeys perform?
The Master’s third question was identical to the previous one.
For a long time, the Tripitaka Master was at a loss as to where [the monk] had gone.
The Master rebuked him, saying,
"You wild fox spirit!"
The Tripitaka Master asked, "Where does the supernormal power of knowing others' minds reside?
Yangshan replied:
Da’er Sanzang asked for the third time, "Why did you not see the National Teacher?
Yangshan replied,
"The previous two times were when your mind was still involved with external objects."
Later, he entered the samādhi of self-enjoyment,
which is why [the monk] did not see him.
Furthermore, there was a monk who cited the previous words and questioned Xuansha.
Xuansha said, "Tell me,
did you see him on those two previous occasions?
Xuanjue replied:
If you saw it during the previous two occasions, why do you not see it now?
Tell me, where does the point of significance lie?
A monk asked Zhaozhou,
"The Great-Eared Tripitaka Master failed to see the National Teacher for the third time.
I wonder where the National Teacher was?"
Zhaozhou said,
"It is upon the nostrils of the Tripitaka.
A monk asked Xuansha:
Since it is right upon the nostrils,
why do you not see it? Xuansha said:
It was simply because he was too close. One day he called to his attendant;
the attendant responded.
He called thus three times, and each time the attendant responded.
The Master said,
"I thought I was failing you,
but it is actually you who are failing me. A monk asked Xuansha:
The National Teacher called to his attendant; what was the meaning of this?
Xuansha said, "In fact, it was the attendant who understood."
Yunju Xi said: "Now tell me, does the attendant understand or not?
If you say he understands..."
The National Teacher further said, "You have failed me.
If you say you do not understand,
Xuansha also said that it was actually the attendant who understood.
Furthermore, how shall one deliberate upon this?
Xuangjue questioned a monk:
"What is the point at which the attendant attained realization?"
The monk said,
"If you do not understand, how can you respond in such a manner? Xuangjue replied,
"You have little understanding."
It is also said:
"If you can reach a resolution here,
then you will see Xuansha."
A monk asked Fayan,
"What was the meaning behind the National Teacher calling for his attendant? Fayan said:
"Go now; come at another time.
Yunju Xi said, "Fayan spoke thus."
Furthermore, does this clarify the National Teacher’s intent, or does it fail to clarify the National Teacher’s intent?
A monk asked Zhaozhou,
"What was the National Teacher’s meaning when he called for his attendant?"
Zhaozhou said, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark;
though the characters themselves do not take shape, their traces are already manifest. Nanquan arrived to pay his respects.
The Master asked,
"Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi."
The Master said,
"Have you brought the portrait of Master Ma?
He replied, "This very one is it."
The Master said, "The one behind you.
Nanquan then ceased speaking. Changqing Ling said:
Baofu Zhan said, "It seems you do not know very well.
You nearly did not come to this place of yours, Master."
Yunju Xi said: "These two venerable ones both support him from behind;
it is only when Nanquan rests that he is truly at ease."
Whether he was supporting Mañjuśrī before him or Maitreya behind him, Magu arrived for an audience, circumambulated the meditation seat three times, and stood before the Master shaking his staff.
The Master said, "Since it is already so, what need is there to see me again?"
Magu again shook his staff;
the Master rebuked him, saying,
"You wild fox spirit, get out!"
The Master would often address the assembly, saying:
"Students of the Chan school should follow the Buddha’s words of the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle to accord with the source of their own minds."
Those who do not understand the provisional meaning do not accord with one another,
like the parasites within a lion's body. Indeed,
if one who serves as a teacher for others becomes entangled in fame and profit, [they fail their duty].
If one opens up heterodox paths, what benefit is there for oneself or others?
Just as a master craftsman’s axe and adze do not injure his hands,
and what a fragrant elephant can carry is not something a donkey can endure.
A monk asked, "How can one attain Buddhahood?
The Master said:
The Buddha and sentient beings simultaneously let go, attaining liberation right where they are.
[A monk] asked, "How can one attain resonance?
The Master said:
Without contemplating good or evil, one spontaneously perceives the Buddha-nature.
Question: How does one attain realization of the Dharmakāya?
The Master said:
"Transcending the realm of Vairocana—
how can one attain what is called the pure Dharma-body?
The Master said:
"Do not seek the Buddha by being attached to him.
[The student] asked, "Which one is the Buddha?
The Master said:
"The very mind is Buddha.
[The questioner] asked, "Does the mind have afflictions?
The Master said:
"The nature of afflictions is itself detached.
[The student] asked, "Is it not that they are severed?
The Master said:
Those who sever the afflictions are called followers of the Two Vehicles.
The non-arising of afflictions is termed Great Nirvāṇa.
Question: Regarding sitting in meditation and observing stillness, how should this be practiced?
The Master said:
"Neither defiled nor pure—
why should you stir the mind to look for signs of purity?"
He asked again,
"Does the Chan Master perceive the empty space of the ten directions as the Dharmakāya?
The Master replied:
To grasp it with a conceptualizing mind is a perverted view.
A question was asked: "If the mind itself is the Buddha, may one still cultivate the myriad practices?
The Master said:
All the noble ones are endowed with the two types of adornment;
how could they deny cause and effect?
Furthermore, it says:
If I were to answer you now, I would not reach the end even after an entire kalpa;
it can be said that you are far removed from the Way.
Therefore, it is said:
To preach the Dharma with the notion of something to be attained is the howling of a jackal;
to preach the Dharma without the notion of anything to be attained is called the lion’s roar.
The practitioner Zhang Fen of Nanyang asked:
"I have humbly heard that you, O Master, speak of 'insentient things preaching the Dharma.
I, however, have not yet realized the meaning of this matter."
"I beg the Master to grant me an instruction.
The Master said,
"If you ask about 'insentient beings preaching the Dharma'..."
"Only by understanding that the insentient can preach the Dharma can one hear my teaching of the Dharma.
You need only go and listen to the insentient preaching the Dharma. Fen said:
"Within the very means available to sentient beings at this moment,
what is the causal condition for the insentient?
The Master said:
Now, within all movements and activities,
there is not even the slightest arising or ceasing in either of the two streams— the mundane or the sagely.
This is precisely what it means for consciousness to transcend and not belong to existence or non-existence.
Vividly perceiving and awakening,
one hears only and has no emotional consciousness or clinging attachment.
Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch said:
The six sense organs encountering their objects and making distinctions are not consciousness.
A monk came to pay his respects;
the Master asked him:
"What practice do you engage in?
He replied, "I lecture on the Diamond Sutra.
The Master said:
"What are the first two characters?
He replied, "Thus (Evam).
The Master said:
What is non-obstructive?
Someone asked: "What is liberation?"
The Master said, "All dharmas do not reach one another; they are liberated in their own place.
[The student] asked, "If that is so, then they must be severed?"
The Master said, "I told you that all dharmas do not reach one another; what is there to cut off?
The Master saw a monk approaching.
He formed a circular shape with his hand and wrote the character for "sun" within it;
the monk had no reply.
The Master questioned Chan Master Benjing:
"In the future, when you encounter extraordinary words, how will you respond? Benjing replied:
"I shall have not a single thought of attachment."
The Master said,
"This is a matter within your own house.
Emperor Suzong asked:
"What dharma has the Master attained?
The Master said,
"Your Majesty, do you see that single cloud in the sky?"
The Emperor said, "I see.
The Master said,
"It is nailed down and hung up."
He asked again,
"What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies?
The Master then rose and said:
"Do you understand? He replied, "I do not.
The Master said:
He handed the old monk a water pitcher and said,
"What is the samādhi of non-contention?"
The Master said,
"Donor, you have walked upon the crown of Vairocana's head.
[The donor] asked, "What is the meaning of this?"
The Master said,
"Do not mistake this for your own pure dharmakāya.
He then asked the Master again.
The Master did not look at him at all and said, "I am the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang;
why do you not deign to look at me?"
The Master said,
"Do you see the void? He replied, "I see it."
The Master said,
