this is called Bodhi.
It is precisely this original source, the pure mind.
Together with all sentient beings, the worlds of the Buddhas, and the mountains and rivers—whether with form or without form—it pervades the realms of the ten directions.
All are equal, devoid of the marks of "self" and "other.
This is the fundamentally pure mind of the source.
It is eternally self-perfected, luminous, and all-illuminating.
Yet worldly people do not awaken to this; they merely identify the faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as the mind, and are thus shrouded by these very functions.
Therefore, one greatly beholds the essence of pure brilliance;
it is simply that when the mind is directly set aside, the essential body manifests of itself.
It is like the great sun-disk rising in the void, illuminating the ten directions without further obstruction.
Therefore, practitioners of the Way mistakenly take seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to be the functioning of the mind.
By emptying out these faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
the path of the mind is cut off and there is no place for entry.
One simply recognizes the original mind within the spheres of seeing,
hearing, sensing, and knowing; yet the original mind does not belong to seeing,
hearing, sensing, and knowing, nor is it separate from them.
Do not give rise to views or interpretations based on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Do not stir thoughts regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Nor should you seek the mind apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Furthermore, do not abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing to grasp at dharmas;

neither identical nor separate, neither abiding nor clinging, moving freely in all directions, there is nothing that is not a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). When worldly people hear of the Way...
All Buddhas transmit the Dharma of the mind. Yet,
one might suppose that there is a separate dharma apart from the mind that can be realized or grasped,
and thus seek the dharma by means of the mind.
One does not realize that the mind is itself the Dharma and the Dharma is itself the mind.
One cannot take the mind to further seek the mind;
even after passing through ten million kalpas, there will never be a day of attainment.
It is better to simply be without mind in the present moment; this is the original Dharma.
It is like the jewel on a strongman’s forehead, hidden within his brow, yet he travels throughout the ten directions seeking it outwardly.
In the end, he could not find it.
A wise person pointed it out to him,
and at that moment, he saw his original jewel there as before.
Practitioners of the Way are deluded regarding their own fundamental mind and do not recognize it as Buddha;
consequently, they seek outwardly, giving rise to practices of effortful cultivation and attempting to realize the stages of fruition according to a gradual sequence.
Even if one diligently seeks throughout kalpas, the Way will not be realized;
it is better to be mindless in the present moment,
decisively knowing that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and unattainable.
Without abiding, without reliance, without capacity, and without object—
when deluded thoughts do not stir, one immediately realizes Bodhi.
Upon realizing the Way, one realizes nothing other than the Buddha of the original mind.
The efforts expended throughout kalpas are all in vain;
it is like a strongman who, upon obtaining the jewel,
finds he has only recovered the one originally on his forehead.
Because it does not depend on the power of seeking outwardly,
the Buddha said:
"Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have truly attained nothing."
Fearing that people might not believe it, he cites the five statements of what is seen by the five eyes.
What is spoken is true and not false; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). O practitioners of the Way, do not harbor doubts.
The four great elements constitute the body;
the four great elements are without self,
and the self likewise has no master.
Therefore, one knows that this body is without self and without a master;
the five aggregates are without self and without a master.
Thus, one knows that this mind is without self and without a master.
The arising and ceasing of the combination of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses is likewise thus.
Since the eighteen realms are empty, all things are entirely empty;
there remains only the fundamental mind, vast and pure.
There is the nutriment of consciousness and the nutriment of wisdom.
When the body composed of the four great elements suffers from the affliction of hunger,
one provides sustenance according to necessity without giving rise to craving or attachment.
This is called the food of wisdom.
Yet, one indulges the passions to seek flavors and gives rise to false discriminations,
seeking only what suits the palate without developing a sense of weary detachment.
This is called the nutriment of consciousness.
As for "śrāvaka," one who attains awakening by means of sound is called a śrāvaka.
However, failing to understand one's own mind,
one gives rise to understanding based on vocal teachings,
or perhaps through supernatural powers.
Or, due to auspicious signs, speech, or movements,
they may hear that there is Bodhi and Nirvana, and that one attains the Buddha-way after practicing for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
all such [teachings] belong to the path of the Śrāvakas.
These are called śrāvakas.
The Buddha, however, directly and immediately realized that his own mind is fundamentally the Buddha;
there is not a single dharma to be attained.
There is not a single practice to be cultivated;
this is the unsurpassed path.
This is the Buddha of True Suchness.
Those who study the Way only fear that a single thought of "existence" will separate them from the Way.
To maintain every thought as signless and every thought as non-active is itself Buddhahood.
If a practitioner of the Way wishes to attain Buddhahood,
they need not study any of the Buddha-dharmas at all;
they should only study non-seeking and non-attachment.
When there is no seeking, the mind does not arise;
when there is no attachment, the mind is not defiled.
This non-arising and non-defilement is itself the Buddha.
The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates correspond to the eighty-four thousand afflictions;
these are gates for teaching and guiding others.
Fundamentally, there is not a single dharma.
Detachment is itself the Dharma;
he who knows detachment is the Buddha.
Merely to be detached from all afflictions is such that no dharma can be apprehended. Those who study the Path who wish to know the essential secret should understand this.
Simply do not allow a single thing to cling to the mind.
To say that the Buddha-dharmakāya is like empty space is a metaphor for the dharmakāya being identical to empty space.
Space is itself the Dharma-body.
Ordinary people assume that the Dharma-body pervades the expanse of space,
as if space were the container and the Dharma-body its content.
One does not realize that space is the Dharmakāya and the Dharmakāya is space.
If one were to definitively say that space exists, [it would be a misconception].
If space were not the Dharmakāya, one would certainly have to say that the Dharmakāya exists;
yet if the Dharmakāya were not space, it would not be so.
Yet one does not form the conceptualization of it as space;
space is itself the Dharma-body.
One does not form the conceptualization of it as the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is identical to space;
space and the Dharma-body have no differing characteristics.
Buddhas and sentient beings have no differing characteristics.
Samsara and nirvana have no different characteristics;
afflictions and bodhi have no different characteristics.
To be free from all characteristics is itself the Buddha.
Ordinary people grasp at objects;
practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind.
When both mind and object are forgotten, that is the true Dharma.
It is relatively easy to forget external objects, but it is extremely difficult to forget the mind.
People do not dare to forget the mind because they fear falling into emptiness, where there is nothing to grasp or perceive.

One does not know that emptiness is fundamentally without emptiness; there is only the single realm of true reality. This nature of numinous awareness has, since time without beginning, shared the same lifespan as empty space;
it has never been born and has never ceased.
Never having existed, never having been non-existent;
never defiled, never pure;
never clamorous, never tranquil.
It has never been young and never been old;
it has no location and no interior or exterior;
it has no quantity and no form or appearance.
It has no form or appearance and no sound;
it cannot be sought, nor can it be grasped;
it cannot be understood through intellectual cognition.
It cannot be grasped through words;
it cannot be met through objects and phenomena;
it cannot be reached through effort.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, together with all sentient beings who move and stir, share the same nature of Great Nirvana.
This nature is the mind;
the mind is the Buddha.
The Buddha is itself the Dharma.
A single thought that deviates from reality is entirely delusion;
one must not seek the mind further within the mind.
One cannot seek the Buddha by means of the Buddha,
nor can one seek the Dharma by means of the Dharma. Therefore,
the practitioner of the Way directly and immediately realizes through mindless, silent resonance.
To conceive a thought is already a deviation.
To transmit mind by means of mind is the correct view.
Be careful not to pursue external objects as the mind.
This is to mistake a thief for one's own son.
Because of the existence of greed, hatred, and delusion, one establishes precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
yet, since afflictions are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be bodhi?
Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to eliminate all mental states."
I have no mind at all;
what use have I for any phenomena?
The source is fundamentally pure; upon the Buddha, one cannot further attach even a single thing.
It is like space:
even if adorned with immeasurable treasures,
it can never be made to abide therein.
The Buddha-nature is identical to empty space;
even though it is adorned with immeasurable wisdom and merit,
it can ultimately never be made to abide.
It is simply that one is deluded regarding one's original nature and thus fails to see it. What is called the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground:
all phenomena are established in reliance upon this mind;
they exist whenever they encounter an object.
When there is no object, there is nothing at all.
One must not exclusively interpret the pure nature as an object.
What is called the function of concentration and wisdom is vividly clear, profoundly still, and alertly aware.
Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing all constitute conceptual understanding directed toward objects;
this may suffice for temporary instruction of those of middling or inferior capacity. However, if one wishes to realize it through direct personal experience:
None of these should be understood in such a way;
they are all bonds of the objective realm.
Phenomena have places where they subside, subsiding within the planes of existence.
One simply does not form views of existence regarding any phenomena;
this is seeing the Dharma. When Master Daomai arrived in China, he spoke only of the single nature.
He transmits only a single Dharma.
He transmits Buddha-to-Buddha and does not speak of other Buddhas;
he transmits Dharma-to-Dharma and does not speak of other Dharmas.
The Dharma is the Dharma that cannot be spoken;
the Buddha is the Buddha that cannot be grasped.
This is precisely the fundamentally pure mind of the source.
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real.
Prajñā is wisdom; this wisdom is the very foundation of formlessness. Ordinary people do not incline toward the Way.
Only by indulging the six sense-faculties does one traverse the six realms of existence.
Thus, after having studied the Way,
one contemplates birth and death in a single thought-moment.
One immediately falls into the paths of the various Māras.
If a single thought-moment gives rise to various views,
one immediately falls into the ways of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
To perceive that there is arising and then its cessation is to fall into the path of the śrāvaka;
it is not to see arising, but only to see cessation.
This is the path of the pratyekabuddha:
phenomena are fundamentally unborn and do not perish now;
one does not give rise to dualistic views, neither feeling aversion nor delight.
All phenomena are nothing but the single mind;
this is then the Buddha-vehicle. Ordinary people all give rise to the mind by pursuing external objects, and their minds follow along with liking and disliking.
If one wishes for there to be no objects, one should forget the mind.
When the mind is forgotten, objects become empty;
when objects are empty, the mind is extinguished.
To eliminate objects while failing to forget the mind is impossible;
it will only serve to increase confusion and agitation.
Therefore, all phenomena are mind-only, and even this mind cannot be apprehended.
What, then, is there to seek? For one who studies the Prajñāpāramitā, not a single dharma can be found.
One should sever all intention toward the three vehicles;
there is but one true reality,
which cannot be realized or attained.
Those who say, "I can realize it" or "I can attain it," are all people of overweening pride (adhimāna).
This refers to those who swept their robes and departed from the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
All these are merely common folk.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"In regard to bodhi, I have truly attained nothing."

It is a matter of silent resonance alone. When ordinary people wish to cultivate and realize the truth, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty and the four elements are without self;
the true mind is signless, neither departing nor arriving.
At the time of birth, its nature does not come;
at the time of death, its nature does not go.
It is profoundly still and perfectly quiescent, with mind and environment as one.
If one can simply realize this directly and instantaneously,
being no longer bound by the three periods of time,
one is then a person who has transcended the world.
One must not have even the slightest inclination or aspiration toward anything.
Even if one sees auspicious signs such as the Buddhas coming to welcome one,
or various manifestations appearing before one, one should have no intention of following them away.
If one sees various evil omens manifesting before them, one remains without fear;
by simply forgetting the self-mind so that it becomes identical with the Dharma-realm, one immediately attains mastery. ○ Generally, what is called a "transformed city" (pura-kṛtaka) refers to...
The two vehicles, the ten stages, and even the levels of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are all provisional establishments of teachings for the purpose of guidance;
they are all "transformed cities."
As for what is called the "place of treasure," it refers to the treasure of the self-nature of the true mind, the fundamental Buddha.
This treasure does not belong to the realm of emotional or intellectual measurement.
It cannot be established;
there is no Buddha and no sentient beings;
there is neither subject nor object.
Where is the city? If one asks this, since it is already a conjured city, where is the place of the treasure?
The place of the treasure cannot be pointed out.
The finger points directly to the place where the treasure is;
it is not the actual place itself.
Therefore, it is said that [the treasure] is merely "nearby."
Regarding what is near,
it cannot be defined by fixed measures;
one should simply realize and accord with it as it is.
An icchantika is one who lacks faith.
All sentient beings of the six realms,
as well as those of the two vehicles, do not believe that there is the fruit of Buddhahood.
All such people are called icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness.
The bodhisattva has deep faith in the Buddha-dharma;
they do not perceive a distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, for Buddhas and sentient beings share the same single dharma-nature.
These are called icchantikas with roots of goodness.
Generally speaking, those who attain awakening through the teachings of sound are called śrāvakas;
those who attain awakening by contemplating causes and conditions are called pratyekabuddhas.
If one does not awaken within one's own mind,
even upon attaining Buddhahood, one is still called a Śrāvaka Buddha.
A student of the Way awakens regarding phenomena, but does not awaken regarding the mind.
Though one may practice through kalpas,
it will ultimately not be the fundamental Buddha;
if there is no awakening within the mind, then one awakens only to the phenomena.
This is to treat the mind lightly while regarding the Dharma as weighty;
it thus results in merely chasing after clods of earth,
for one has forgotten their original mind.
Simply accord with the fundamental mind and do not seek the Dharma;
the mind is itself the Dharma. Ordinary people often say that objects obstruct the mind, or that phenomena obstruct principle.
One constantly desires to flee from objects in order to settle the mind, and to screen out affairs in order to preserve principle.
One does not realize that this is actually the mind obstructing objects and principle obstructing affairs;
one need only allow the mind to be empty, and the objects will naturally become empty.
Simply ensure that when principle is quiescent, phenomena are naturally quiescent;
do not apply the mind perversely. Ordinary people often refuse to empty their minds, fearing they will fall into nihilism, yet they do not realize that their own minds are fundamentally empty.
The foolish person eliminates external affairs but does not eliminate the mind;
the wise person eliminates the mind but does not eliminate external affairs.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is like space, relinquishing everything.
One does not cling to any merit performed.
Furthermore, there are three levels of relinquishment:
relinquishing everything, including the internal and external, body and mind.
It is like space, which has nothing to grasp or cling to;
thereafter, in accordance with circumstances and responding to beings, both subject and object are forgotten—
this is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
If one practices the path and cultivates virtue on one side,
while on the other side one turns away with no expectation,
this state of mind is called "middle equanimity."
If one extensively cultivates various virtues while harboring expectations,
yet upon hearing the Dharma realizes emptiness and consequently becomes unattached, this is called "minor relinquishment."
Great equanimity is like a torch held before one; there is no further confusion or awakening.
Intermediate equanimity is like a torch held at one's side;
it may be bright or dim.
Minor relinquishment is like a torch held behind one, for one does not see the pits and pitfalls;
the bodhisattva’s mind is like space,
relinquishing everything.
The past mind cannot be apprehended;
this is the relinquishing of the past.
The present mind cannot be apprehended.
This is present relinquishment;
the future mind is unobtainable,
and this is future relinquishment.
This refers to the simultaneous relinquishing of the three periods of time.
Ever since the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa, it has been transmitted from mind to mind by means of the seal of the mind.
Mind and mind are not different.
If a seal is applied to emptiness, the seal does not form a character;
if a seal is applied to a material object, the seal does not form a dharma.
Therefore, one uses the mind to seal the mind, yet mind and mind are not different.
Since that which seals and that which is sealed are both difficult to bring into accord,
those who attain it are few.
However, where the mind is absent, there is no gaining of the mind; where there is no gaining, there is no attainment. The Buddha has three bodies:
the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) teaches the dharma of the self-nature’s spiritual penetration;
the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) teaches all pure dharmas.
The Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) preaches the Dharma of the six perfections and the myriad practices.
The Dharmakāya (Dharma Body) preaches the Dharma not by means of speech, sound, form, or written characters;
it has nothing to preach and nothing to realize.
It is simply the spontaneous penetration of intrinsic nature.
Therefore it is said:
"There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called teaching the Dharma."
The teachings manifested by the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) all appear according to the perceptions and capacities of sentient beings;
they are also adapted to specific circumstances and faculties for the purpose of gathering and transforming them.
None of these, however, constitute the True Dharma.

Therefore it is said: "The retributive and transformational bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. As for what was said regarding "the same single brilliant essence being divided into six harmonious combinations":
"the single brilliant essence" refers to the one mind.
The six conjunctions refer to each of the six sense faculties conjoining with its respective object:
the eye conjoins with form;
the ear conjoins with sound.
The nose meets with odors;
the tongue meets with flavors;
the body meets with tangibles.
When the mind and mental objects come together,
the six consciousnesses arise in between, forming the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
If one thoroughly understands that these eighteen elements are empty and non-existent, [one realizes their true nature].
The six harmonious aggregates are bound together as a single refined essence.
This single refined essence is precisely the mind;
those who study the Way all know this.
Yet they cannot avoid forming an interpretation based on intellectual cleverness and the six harmonies;
consequently, they are bound by the Dharma and fail to accord with their original mind.
Thus, the Tathāgata, appearing in this world, desires to expound the true Dharma of the One Vehicle.
If [the Buddha] did not speak, sentient beings would lack faith, give rise to slander, and sink into the ocean of suffering.
If he were to remain entirely silent, the Buddha would fall into stinginess and greed,
failing to universally bestow the wondrous Way upon sentient beings.
Consequently, he skillfully taught the three vehicles;
as these vehicles have degrees of greatness or smallness and attainments of depth or shallowness,
none of them constitute the fundamental Dharma.
Therefore it is said:
"Only this One Vehicle path is true; the other two are not real.
Yet, even so, it has not yet been able to manifest the Dharma of the One Mind.
Therefore, he summoned Kāśyapa to sit together upon the same Dharma-seat and separately entrusted him with the teaching of the single mind that transcends words.
This branch of the Dharma is now practiced separately.
If one can realize this through awakening, one immediately reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
The Verse on Transmitting the Mind by Prime Minister Pei Xiu: I personally received instruction from Chan Master Huangbo Xiyun at both Wanling and Zhongling.
Having fully transmitted the essentials of the mind,
he then composed these Verses on the Transmission of Mind.
Yet, the mind cannot be transmitted.
Take the seal as the transmission;
the mind cannot be seen,
but it is seen through non-action.
The seal is also without a seal;
non-existence is also without non-existence.
The conjured city is not a place of abiding.
The summit of Mount Meru possesses a jewel;
"jewel" is but a provisional designation.
How could a city have a physical form?
"The very mind is Buddha;
Buddha is non-arising.
It is right here and now."
Do not seek, do not strive;
to cause the Buddha to search for the Buddha would only double the expenditure of effort.
To give rise to understanding based on following dharmas is to fall into the realm of Māra; therein,
the ordinary and the sage are not distinguished.
Thus, one departs from seeing and hearing;
with no-mind resembling a mirror,
one does not compete with things.
Non-thought is like space;
there is nothing it does not accommodate.
It transcends the dharmas of the Three Vehicles.
Rarely encountered throughout kalpas;
if one can act thus, such a person is a hero who has transcended the world.
I have heard that the Great Master of Hedong personally witnessed the High An Teacher transmit the essentials of the mind;
in that year, he composed verses and chapters to show them to future generations.
Suddenly the deaf and blind were opened;
it was as brilliant as a painting in vermilion and green. I regret what has been lost.
This is appended to the original record.
In the year Wuzi of the Qingli era, one named Nanzong Zhitianzhen inscribed this on the *Chuanxin fayao*, revising eleven locations:
three characters were deleted and nine characters were added.
This is based on the records of the four houses as well as the separate records. *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Scroll Nine;
*Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Scroll Ten:
Sixty-one persons under the third generation of Chan Master Huairang.
The seventeen Dharma heirs of Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of Chizhou were:
Chan Master Jingcen of Changsha in Hunan; Chan Master Tanzhao of Baima in Jingnan; Chan Master Shizu of Yunji on Mount Zhongnan;
Chan Master Yiduan of Xiantang at Xiangyan in Dengzhou; and Dongyuan Cong of Zhaozhou.
The thirteen individuals who met [the Master] were: Chan Master Shen of Chizhou; Chan Master Xian of Lingjiu;
Venerable Master Zhuyushan of Ezhou; Chan Master Lizong of Zihu in Quzhou; Venerable Master Rizhi of Songshan in Luojing;
Venerable Master Xichan of Suzhou; Provincial Governor Lu Xun of Xuanchuan; and the Lay Practitioner Gan Zhi of Chizhou. Above, these are the thirteen.

Recorded are Chan Master Cuzhen of Zishan, Chan Master Daohong of Jiangling, Chan Master Xuanji of Xuanzhou, and Chan Master Daojun of Silla—these four have no recorded机缘 (karmic conditions) or dialogues, so they are not included here.
Recorded are the eight Dharma successors of Chan Master Qian’an of Yanguan in Hangzhou: Chan Master Daochang of Guannan in Xiangzhou; [and] Hongzhou Shuang... [text fragment].
Chan Master Ling Xuanzhen; Chan Master Jiaozong of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou—these three individuals above are recorded [in this collection].
Chan Master Baiyun Tanjing of Emperor Xuanzong’s Tang Dynasty; Chan Master Luxu Wenju of Lu Prefecture;
Chan Master Pimir of Silla; and Chan Master Jianzong of Shouzhou—these five individuals above have no recorded exchanges or dialogues.
Recorded are the four dharma heirs of Chan Master Lingmo of Wuyi Mountain in Wuzhou; one is recorded here: Chan Master Zhengyuan of Guishan in Fuzhou.

Also recorded are Chan Master Xiaofang of Ganquan Temple, Chan Master Zanghuan of Qixin Temple in Mingzhou, and Chan Master Yuansui of Ganquan Temple—these three are not recorded as they lack recorded dialogues or exchanges.
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Ruman of Foguang Temple in the Capital (Luoyang) are one: Bai Juyi, Prefectural Governor of Hangzhou; and one: [recorded in the present collection].
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Fachang of Mount Damei in Mingzhou are three: Chan Master Gazi of the Kingdom of Silla;
and Monk Tianlong of Hangzhou—the above two are recorded in the present collection; and Zhong of the Kingdom of Silla.
Master Yan alone had no recorded机缘 (ji-yuan) or dialogues, so they are not included.
Master Lingtuan of Yongtai Temple in Jingzhou had five dharma heirs: Master Jie Xu of Shanglin in Hunan; the Master of Bimora Cliff on Mount Wutai;
and Master Zhilin of Hunan—these three are already recorded above. Master Wenzhi of Luyoushan is also recorded here.
The two masters above, including Chan Master Fahé of Suzhou, have no recorded *jìyuán* (circumstantial dialogues) or spoken words, so they are not included here.
As for the two successors of Chan Master Bǎojī of Pánshān in Yōuzhōu: the first is Upādhyāya Pùhuà of Zhèn府, whose record is preserved;

the second is Upādhyāya Shàngfāng of Zhènzhōu, who has no recorded *jìyuán* or spoken words and is therefore not included. [The successor] from Xīngshàn Temple in Jīngzhào is Wéi... [text breaks off].
Chan Master Kuān had six dharma heirs: Chan Master Fǎzhì of Jīngzhào; Chan Master Wúbiǎo of Jīngzhào;
Chan Master Huìjiàn of Jīngzhào; Chan Master Yuànjìng of Jīngzhào; Chan Master Huìguāng of Jīngzhào; and Chan Master Yìzōng of Jīngzhào.

As for these six individuals above, since there are no recorded dialogues or exchanges regarding their spiritual capacities, they are not included here. [Also recorded is] Chan Master Jìngzōng of Yúnshuǐ.
He had two Dharma heirs: Chan Master Shenzhao of Xiaoma in Huazhou and Chan Master Daoyuan of Huazhou.
Of these two, as there are no recorded dialogues or exchanges, they are not included here. He also had two Dharma heirs of Chan Master Yuanchang of Longya Mountain in Tanzhou:
Chan Master Zangyi of Jiahe, whose record is preserved here, and Chan Master Zangshu of Yangchang.
As there are no recorded exchanges of questions and answers (ji-yuan yu-jù) for these individuals, they are not included here:
Chan Master Changzhen of Zhenzhou and Chan Master Yì of Fengxian in Zhenzhou—these two aforementioned masters have no recorded exchanges and are thus not recorded.
There were six Dharma heirs of Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu: [the first was] Ling... of Fuyong Mountain in Fuzhou.
Master Xun, Master Gaoteng of Guocheng County in Hannan, Master Daemao of Silla, and Master Zhitong of Mount Wutai—these four are recorded above.

Master Dayu of Gao’an in Hongzhou and Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou—these two have no recorded机缘 (jiyuan) or dialogues and are therefore not recorded. [The record ends with] Baohua of Luzushan.
Master Yun’s Dharma heirs: one, Master Yunshui; one, [whose]机缘 (ji yuán) and recorded sayings are not preserved.
Master Datong of Ziyu Mountain’s Dharma heir: one, Yu Di, the Regional Inspector of Xiangzhou during the Tang dynasty;
[one whose] 机缘 (ji yuán) and recorded sayings are not preserved. Master Zhiyan of Huayan Temple’s Dharma heir: one, Huang...
In the *Chuzi*, the monk Qi’an alone is recorded under the third generation of Huairang.
Regarding the successors of Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of South Pool, Chizhou: there was the Master of Changsha in Hunan, named Jingcen, titled the Great Master Zhaoxian.
Regarding the successors of Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of South Pool, Chizhou: there was the Master of Changsha in Hunan, named Jingcen, titled the Great Master Zhaoxian.
At first, he resided at the Deer Park as his primary dwelling;
thereafter, he had no fixed abode,
but followed conditions to engage with sentient beings, preaching the Dharma wherever he was invited.
Therefore, the assembly at that time called him the "Monk of Changsha.

"Brother, what do you say?
The Master replied, "This beast."
Dajue arrived for an audience.
The Master raised his whisk.
Dajue spread out his sitting mat.
The Master threw down his whisk.
Da-jue gathered up his sitting cloth and entered the Sangha hall.
The assembly of monks said:
"This monk must be a personal acquaintance of the Master;
he neither prostrates nor accepts the staff.
Upon hearing this, the Master ordered the newly arrived monk to be summoned.
Dajue then came out.
The Master said,
"The assembly says you have not yet consulted the Elder."
Dajue said, "I do not understand," and immediately returned to the assembly.
When Magu arrived for his second visit to the world, he spread out his sitting mat and asked:
The Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara faces directly toward Anan.
The Master descends from his rope-seat;
with one hand he gathers up his sitting mat, and with the other he seizes Magu, saying:
"Where has the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara gone?
As Magu turned his body and prepared to sit upon the rope bed,
the Master raised his staff and struck him.
Magu took him by the arm and led him together into the abbot’s quarters.
The Master ascended the hall and said,
"Great assembly!"
"One who practices the Dharma does not shrink from losing body or life.
At the place of my late teacher Huangbo,
I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times."
Three times he received blows from him, as if brushed by a bundle of mugwort; now he thinks further of receiving one more blow—“Who will give me a hand?
At that time, a monk stepped forward and said:
"Such-and-such a person has attained it.
The Master raised his staff and handed it to him;
the monk prepared to receive it.
The Master then struck him. Later, Xuefeng took up this story and said:
"Linji was much like a thief who steals in broad daylight. A monk asked:
"What is the first phrase?"
The Master said:
"The seal of the Three Essentials is opened; the vermilion dot is narrow.
There is no room for deliberation; host and guest are distinguished."
[The student] asked, "What is the second phrase?
The Master said,
"How could wondrous understanding allow for the questions of Asanga?"
Ouhua contended over the mechanism for cutting through the stream.
[The monk] asked, "What is the third phrase?
The Master said:
"Look at the puppeteer on the stage manipulating the puppets;
all the pulling and tugging depends entirely upon those within.
The Master spoke again:
Now, a single phrase must embody the three mysteries;
each mystery must embody the three essentials.
Therein lie both the provisional and the functional.
"How do you all understand this? On the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty (the Bingxu year),
as the Master was about to pass into nirvana, he ascended the hall and said:
"After my extinction, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
The Three Sages replied,
"How would we dare extinguish the Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?"
The Master said,
"If someone asks you about this in the future, what will you say to them?
Sansheng then gave a shout.
The Master said,
"Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by this blind donkey?
He then spoke a verse:
Following the stream without ceasing, I ask: what is it like? True illumination is boundless; let me explain it to you.
Beyond form and beyond name, it is not received by anyone. The "blow-off blade" has been used; when urgent, it must be sharpened again.
Having finished this verse, he sat and passed away.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Huizhao;
his stupa was named Chengling. *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, Scroll 13.
Including Chan Master Huairang and those who branched out from Caoxi, there are seventy-seven persons in total:
eleven generations from the seventh to the ninth generation of Chan Master Huairang, and five generations from the second to the sixth generation of the Caoxi branch.
Regarding the "eleven persons" of the seventh generation [of Huairang], one version reads "ninth generation"; this refers to Bajiaoshan in Yingzhou.

The four Dharma heirs of Chan Master Huiqing are as follows: Chan Master Qingrang of Xingyang in Yingzhou and Chan Master Faman of Yougushan in Hongzhou—these two are recorded in the present collection.
Chan Master Yishen of Xingyang in Yingzhou and Chan Master Zhiyu, the second abbot of Bajiaoshan—these two are not recorded here, as they lacked recorded dialogues or exchanges.
The four Dharma heirs of Chan Master Rizhao of Zifu in Jizhou were:
Chan Master Zhengsui of Zifu in Jizhou, Venerable Fushou of Jizhou, and Venerable Luyuan of Tanzhou. The records for these three masters have already been included above.
Master Deshao of Baoci in Tanzhou had no recorded机缘 (karmic conditions) or spoken words, and thus he is not recorded here. [The record continues with] Venerable He of Baoying in Ruzhou.
Shangfa had one successor, namely Nanyuan Yong. Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue in Ruzhou;
Chan Master Siming of Xiyan in Ruzhou—these two each had one successor recorded in the present collection:
Chan Master Guijing of Xingyang in Yingzhou and Chan Master Hongjiu of Huilin in Shaoyou. The master of Lingrui in Shaoyou also had one successor recorded in the present collection.
The Eighth Generation from Huairang: Six Masters. The four dharma heirs of Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue in Ruzhou:
Chan Master Zhen of Guanghui in Ruzhou; Chan Master Shengnian of Shoushan in Ruzhou—the above two are recorded in the [Feng]fenglu;
Master Changxing of Fengxiang; and Master Lingquan of Tanzhou—the above two have no recorded机缘 (jiyuan) dialogues.
The verses are not recorded here. The two dharma heirs of Master Guizhen of Baoci in Tanzhou are:
Chan Master Zhiqian of Sanjiao Mountain in Qizhou and Chan Master Ciduo of Xingyang in Yingzhou.
The one dharma heir of Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian in Ruzhou whose record is currently extant is Chan Master Fenzhou Shenzhao; one other [record] is currently extant as a eulogy.
Attached at the end of this volume: One dharma successor of Master Dingzhen of Mount Luofu—Master Lingyun of Mount Luofu;
as there are no recorded机缘 (jiyuan) or spoken words, they are not included. One dharma successor of Master Daojin of Mount Zhikong—Master Xuanjue of Jingzhou;
as there are no recorded机缘 or spoken words, he is not included. [Recorded are] Shan of Huitian in Shaoyou.
Master Kuai had one Dharma heir, Chan Master Shanwu; as there are no recorded机缘 (ji yuán) or dialogues, they are not included here.
Master Benjing of Sikongshan had one Dharma heir, the Imperial Envoy Yang Guangting; as there are no recorded机缘 or dialogues, they are not included here.
Master Yuansu had two Dharma heirs: Chan Master Xiaodao Jin of Shaoyou Prefecture... [and another].
The above two individuals, including Chan Master Youji of Shaoyou Prefecture, had no recorded *gong'an* (critical exchanges) or dialogues; they are not included here.
Zen Master Daqian of Hengzhou was the sole successor of National Teacher Zhishen of Jetavana; he also had no recorded *gong'an* or dialogues and is not included.
There were five successors of National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang; one is currently recorded here: Zhen of Mount Danyuan in Jizhou.

Master Yingchan (of the Tang Dynasty), Emperor Suzong of the Tang, Emperor Daizong of the Tang, Sun Zhigu of Kaifeng, and Master Xiangyan Weijie of Dengzhou—these four individuals have no recorded exchanges of spiritual inquiry (*jìyuán*) or dialogues, and thus are not included here.
As for the eighteen dharma heirs of Grand Master Shenhui of Hozhai in Luoyang, two of them are recorded below: [the first is] Dashi Shan of Huangzhou.
Chan Master Fulin; Chan Master Guangbao of Mount Meng in Yishui; Chan Master Faru of Cizhou;
Chan Master Jinping of Mount Xiyin in Huai'an Prefecture; Chan Master Huiyan of Liyang; Chan Master Huaikong of Heyang;
Chan Master Yuanzhen of Nanyang; Chan Master Guangfu of Yichun; Chan Master Xingjue of Jiangling; and [the masters of] Wutai.
Shanshen Ying Chan Master; Wuming Chan Master of Mount Wutai; Haoyu Chan Master of Mount Nanyue;
Zhiman Chan Master of Xuanzhou; Lang Chan Master of Fuzhou; Lingtan Chan Master of Guangling; Tongyin Chan Master of Ningzhou; Nan Yin Chan Master of Yizhou;
and Li Chang, the Governor of Henan—these sixteen individuals were without the [karmic] capacity [for this teaching].
As for the recorded sayings and phrases, they are not included here; they have been separately published in the *Caohēi* (Record of Caoxi). Under the third generation, nine individuals are listed.
Regarding the successor to Chan Master Huántián Shànwù, Tánzhōu Wúxué Chánshī—one person—there are no recorded机缘 (circumstantial dialogues) or sayings, so they are not included.
Regarding the successor to Wángshān Dàojiàn Héshàng, Húnán Rúbǎo Chánshī—one person—there are no recorded机缘 or sayings, so they are not included.
Recorded: One successor of Master Zhenyi of Danyuan Mountain, Chan Master Zhengsui of Jizhou;
as there are no recorded机缘 (jiyuan) or spoken words, he is not further recorded. One successor of Master Faru of Cizhou, Chan Master Weizhong of Jingnan;
as there are no recorded机缘 or spoken words, he is not further recorded. Successor of Master Huai Kong of Heyang, Daoming of Caizhou.
As for Zen Master Yuanzhen of Wuya Mountain, a successor of Zen Master Fazhi of Mount Simian (the "Four Sides" mountain) and the Rhetu Daowei of Wu:
as these two individuals have no recorded dialogues or sayings, they are not included here.
As for the one successor of Zen Master Wuming of Mount Wutai: it is Grand Master Chengguan of Huayan on Mount Wutai.
One person had no recorded机缘 (ji jian) or sayings; they are not included. Master Nanyin of Yizhou was the successor of one person, Chan Master Yifu;
one person had no recorded *ji jian* or sayings and is not included. From Caoxi, there is a separate lineage of the fourth generation consisting of five people.
Four were the successors of Chan Master Weizhong of Jingnan; Chan Master Zhong was also named Nan-yin Daoyuan.
Chan Master Ru Yi of Yizhou; Chan Master Shen Zhao of Fengguo; Chan Master Ya of Donglin on Mount Lu—these four masters have no recorded exchanges or sayings, so they are not included.
Regarding the single successor of the Ruhu Tuo: Chan Master Xuan Gu. This one also has no recorded exchanges or sayings, so he is not included.
These are the four [masters] of the fifth generation of the separate line from Caoxi.
The one successor of Chan Master Daoyuan of Suzhou whose records survive is Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan.
The successors of Chan Master Shenzhao of Fengguo are Chan Master Changyi of Zhenzhou, Chan Master Zhiyuan of Huazhou, and Chan Master Xuansui of Lutaishan;
as these three have no recorded机缘 (ji yuan) dialogues or sayings, they are not included here.
The sixth generation of this lineage branch consists of eleven individuals: Chan Master Guifeng Weng, Dharma successor of Chan Master Guifeng Zongmi;
Chan Master Taigong of Cien Monastery; Chan Master Taixi of Xingshan Monastery;
Chan Master Zong of Wansheng Monastery; Chan Master Jue of Ruisheng Monastery; and Chan Master Renyu of Huadu Monastery—these six aforementioned masters.
No records of机缘 (karmic conditions) or recorded sayings for Master Luntai Xuansui; his sole dharma successor was Master Longxing Nian.
No records of机缘 or recorded sayings for him. The successors of Master Huazhou Zhiyuan were:
Master Pengmen Shen Yong, Master Yuanshao, Master Shangfang Zhen, and Master Dongjing Fazhi. The above.
The four individuals lacked the karmic conditions for dialogue, so their words are not recorded. The Dharma Heir of the Seventh Generation, Zen Master Huairang:
The Dharma Heir of the Seventh Generation, Zen Master Huiqing of Bajiao Mountain in Former Yingzhou:
Zen Master Qingrang of Xingyang Mountain in Yingzhou. Zen Master Qingrang of Xingyang Mountain in Yingzhou.
The Master asked:
"When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas,
yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood— what was it like then?"
The Master said,
"That question was most profound and appropriate.
The monk said:
"Since you are already seated at the site of enlightenment,
why have you not attained the Buddha-way?
The Master said:
Because he did not become a Buddha. Chan Master Faman of Mount Yougu in Hongzhou.
A monk asked:
"What is the Way? After a long silence, the Master said,
"Do you understand?"
The monk said, "I,
a student, do not understand.
The Master said:
When speech is exhausted, words fall silent;
he has earnestly proclaimed the profound essence.
Grasp this essential teaching of Chan now.
There is no need for further elaboration.

The Dharma successor of the former Chan Master Ribao of Zifu in Jizhou was Chan Master Zhengsui of Zifu in Jizhou. Regarding Chan Master Zhengsui of Zifu in Jizhou, during his second term as abbot, a monk asked:
The Master asked, "Seeing what meaning did the ancients obtain that they simply ceased [their practice]?
The Teacher drew a circle and showed it to him.
He then asked, "What is the ancient song?"
The Master drew a circle and showed it to him.
[The student] asked, "What is the very first phrase?
The Master said:
When the world was not yet formed, the *ācārya* was also here.
Baizhang asked, "What was the meaning of rolling up the mat? After a long silence, the Master replied.
Question: "What was the meaning of the ancients saying 'three before, three after'?
The Master said, "What is your name?"
[The monk] said, "So-and-so.
The Master said,
"Go and drink tea."
The Master said to the assembly,
"If one sees the flagpole of Zifu Temple across the river and turns back immediately,
I would give thirty blows to their heels as well."
How much more so when he came across the river;
as soon as a monk emerged, the Master said,
"He is not fit to converse with."
Question: "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha?
The Master said:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth."
Regarding Master Fushou of Jizhou: A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the patriarchs and the meaning of the teachings the same or different?"
The Master then extended his hand and asked:
"Mañjuśrī rides a lion and Samantabhadra rides an elephant;
I wonder, what does Śākyamuni ride?"
The Master raised his hand and said,
"Xie xie! The Venerable Master of Lùyuàn in Tánzhōu, the Venerable Master of Lùyuàn in Tánzhōu."
A monk asked,
"When one becomes a Buddha in other lands, is there still a different name?
The Master drew a circle and showed it to him.
Question: "What is the single path of the Deer Park?
The Master said:
"Bring forth the tongue of Jiaoliao and ask."
Question: "What is it like?
The Master said: "Building a carriage while shut inside one's door."
At the Stone Bridge of Nanyue,
a monk asked,
"What is it like to follow the same tracks when leaving the gate?"
The Master said,
"The tip of the staff and the shoe.
The Master ascended the hall and, extending his hands, said:
"The life-force of all the elder monks and venerable seniors in the world is entirely contained right here.
A monk stepped forward and asked,
"Have you gathered it back yet?"
The Master said,
"Beside the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
The monk said, "I do not think so."
The Master said,
"I humbly pray that you may accept this offering.
He then asked, "What is the meaning of 'that which the World-Honored One did not speak'?"
The Master said,
"Mount Sumeru has collapsed.
[The student] asked, "What is 'Kāśyapa hearing what cannot be heard'?"
The Master said:
"The great ocean has dried up.
[This refers to] the Dharma heir of the late Master Baoying of Ruizhou; he was also known as Nan'uan. Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue, Ruizhou, was a native of Yuhang.
He first set out from Yuezhou under the Great Master Jingqing Shunde,
but before he had reached the inner sanctum,
he subsequently traveled to Huayan Monastery in Lizhou.
He encountered a man sitting on the corridor who was a servant of Nan-yuan of Ruzhou;
he then secretly investigated Nan-yuan’s fundamental tenets.
Later, when he arrived at Nan-yuan, he did not prostrate upon first seeing him;
instead, he asked,
"Upon entering the gate, one must discern the master."
"I truly request that the Master distinguish this for me.
Nan-yuan patted his knee with his left hand.
The Master shouted.
Nanyuan patted his knee with his right hand.
The Master shouted again.
Nanyuan raised his left hand and said:
"Setting this aside, it comes from the Acharya.
Again, raising his right hand, he said, "And as for this— how is it?"
The Master said, "Blind!
As Nan-yuan was about to pick up his staff,
the Master said:
"What are you doing? he asked,
snatching the staff and striking the old monk,
saying, "Do not say I did not warn you."
Nanyuan said, "I have served as abbot for thirty years,
yet today I am being entangled by this Yellow-Faced One coming to my door.
The Master said:
"The Master is much like one who, unable to hold his almsbowl, falsely claims he is not hungry.
Nan-yuan said, "When did you,
Dharma brother, ever come to Nan-yuan?"
The Master said,
"What words are these? [The monk] replied,
"I, this old monk, am asking you earnestly."
The Master said, "I cannot let this pass. Nan-yuan said,
"Sit for a moment and drink some tea."
The Master was just then performing the rites of teacher and disciple.
Thereafter, responding to the prediction of Miaoyan and Yangshan regarding his emergence in the world to gather disciples,
Nan’uan’s Dharma path spread widely throughout all quarters.
The Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:
"As for the eyes of those who study the Way,
when facing critical moments, you must ensure that the Great Function manifests before you."
Do not confine yourself to minor details.
Even if you were to attain realization prior to words,
it would still be a lingering shell and a deluded enclosure.
Even if you are thoroughly proficient in the words [of the teachings],
you cannot avoid encountering wild views wherever you go. Observe you all!
It must have been that you previously relied on others to form your understanding;
now, both the bright and the dim paths are swept away at once.
This shall ensure that each and every one of you, like a lion cub, lets out a roar with a gaping mouth, standing tall and solitary as a cliff face rising ten thousand fathoms.
"Who would dare look at him with a direct gaze?
To look upon him is to blind one's own eyes.
The Master then proceeded to the government office in Yingzhou.
Ascending the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The mind-seal of the Patriarchs is like the mechanism of an iron ox."
When departing, one is sealed by abiding;
when abiding, one is sealed by breaking.
It is just like neither departing nor abiding.
"Sealing is precisely non-sealing; is it so?
Is there anyone who can say this?
At that time, the Elder Lupi came forward and asked.
"The student possesses the faculty of the 'iron ox';
I request that you, Master, do not affix the seal.
The Master said:
He was accustomed to hooking leviathans in the vast depths of the great ocean;
yet he sighed at the frog’s stride, mired in the mud and sand. Qīnggōng Shìyuàn notes that "frog" (wā) should be read as "deep pool" (wā).
This refers to the horse that emerged from the Wa-wa Waters.
As for what the "Wind Cavern" calls a "stumbling horse," it means that a fine steed emerged from clear water.
Yet it, on the contrary, wallows and lies in the mud and sand;
such is its nature. Now, the commentator records that the term "wa" refers to the shrimp-frog (蝦蟆).
"How could one lie down and sleep for the sake of horses and foot-soldiers?
[The Master] sighed deeply while brooding.
The Master then shouted:
"Elder, why do you not speak? Bi hesitated.
The Master struck him once with his whisk and said:
Do you still remember the *huatou*?
Try to bring it up.
Before Baizhang was about to open his mouth—
The Master struck him once more with his whisk.
The Herdsman said,
"I know for certain that the Buddha-dharma and the royal law are one and the same."
The Master asked,
"What principle have you seen?
The cowherd replied:
"If one fails to sever what ought to be severed, one instead invites chaos.
The Master then descended from his seat.
Upon entering the hall for the formal discourse, a monk asked:
"Whose song does the Master sing? Whom does he succeed in the ancestral style?
The Master replied:
"Transcendent and far-reaching, beyond the realm of Wei-yin."
The *Tiṣya-pūrvayoga-sūtra* states:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Tiṣya."
At that time, there were two bodhisattvas:
the first was named Śākyamuni,
and the second was named Maitreya.
The Buddha perceived that while Śākyamuni’s mind was not yet matured, the minds of his disciples were all fully ripened; he reflected thus:
"The mind of a single person can be easily and swiftly transformed."
"The minds of the multitude are difficult to cure quickly.
He immediately ascended the Snowy Mountains,
entered a jeweled cave, and attained the great meditative absorption (*mahā-dhyāna*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was an ascetic of the non-Buddhist path.

Regarding the "Bamboo-tendon Whip" beneath the Staff Forest (Yaṣṭivana), the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
Formerly, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of Śākyamuni Buddha was one zhang and six chi in height.
Constantly harboring doubts, he did not yet believe it;
he therefore took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff,
intending to measure the Buddha’s body.
The staff constantly extended beyond sixteen feet from its tip;
as it continued to grow taller, its true limit could not be fathomed.
Thereupon, he cast down the staff and departed.
Thus it took root there.
Today, the bamboo groves grow tall and lush, covering the mountains and filling the valleys.

The writings and records of various masters have been transcribed to elucidate the fundamental principles and origins of the Chan school;
these texts, verses, and phrases are compiled into a single canon, or as it is called—
It consists of one hundred fascicles intended to be bequeathed to future generations.
Its general preface states briefly:
"Chan is a term from India."
In its full form, it is called *dhyāna*.
It is translated as "cultivation through reflection" (*sīwéixiū*) and is also called "tranquil contemplation" (*jìnglù*).
These are all general designations for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Source" refers to the fundamentally awakened true nature of all sentient beings.
It is also called Buddha-nature;
it is also called the ground of the mind.
To awaken to it is termed wisdom.
Cultivating this is called concentration (*samādhi*); when concentration and wisdom are taken together, they are termed meditation (*dhyāna*).
This nature is the fundamental source of meditation.
Therefore, it is called the "Source of Dhyāna," and is also named "Dhyāna.
As for the practice of principle:
The fundamental source of this is the principle of dhyāna;
to forget the emotions and accord with it is the practice of dhyāna.
Hence, it is called "principle and practice."
However, among the various works compiled here,

There is a certain kind of monk who sits upon a rope-bench and calls himself a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra).
When questioned, he immediately moves his body, gestures with his hands, points at his eyes, sticks out his tongue, and stares blankly;
furthermore, there is another type who simply says:
"It is this brilliant and numinous spirit, the cognitive faculty of the *lingtai*, which is able to see and hear."
To act as a master within the field of the five aggregates—that is what you call being a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra); it is a great deception of people.
Do you understand? I now ask you:
if you identify with that which is brilliant and lucid, [you are mistaken].
If this were your true reality,
why would it not be vividly clear and alert even during sleep?
If it were not your true reality during sleep, why would there be a time of vivid clarity [while awake]?
Do you understand?
This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son";
it is the root of birth and death, a deluded thought and a condition of karmic energy.
Do you wish to recognize the source of this faculty?
I shall tell you: it is that which is luminous and numinous within you.
It is only because of the dharmas of past sensory objects—such as form, sound, and fragrance—that discrimination arises;
thus you claim this "bright and numinous" awareness is real.
If these external objects did not exist, your bright and numinous awareness would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
"O Benevolent One,
where does true reality reside?
You now wish to attain mastery over the field of the five aggregates and the body of others."
Simply recognize your secret vajra-body.
The ancients said to you:
it is perfectly realized, pervasive, and completely encompassing the entire dharma-realm.
I shall now provide a brief explanation for you, wise one,
so that you may understand it through an analogy.
Do you see this sun over Jambudvīpa in the south?
All the various mental activities and karmic deeds performed by people in the world to sustain their bodies and maintain their lives are established by relying upon the sun's radiance. Yet,
does the essence of the sun itself possess such manifoldness or mental activity?
Is there anything that is not pervaded by this?
If you wish to recognize this adamantine essence, it is just like this:
right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness; as well as your own body and mind.
Is it not all manifested through the pervasive and perfected majestic light you have inherited?

It is simply that among the various classes of heavenly and human beings, there are those who receive the retribution of birth according to their karmic actions—whether they possess a sentient nature or are insentient.
Is it not all received through your majestic radiance?
Even until the Buddhas attain enlightenment, realize the fruit, and engage with beings to benefit them—
all is entirely received through your majestic radiance.
Just as it is with the adamantine body, does it still contain ordinary beings and Buddhas?
Does it have the mental activities of your mind?
You must not say that it is non-existent and thereby presume to attain realization.
Do you understand? Since you possess such extraordinary qualities, why do you not manifest them when facing the light?
Instead, you merely follow others in making a living within the field of the five aggregates and the realm of ghosts.
While you are thus directly deceiving yourself,
suddenly the realm of impermanence and death will arrive,
and your eyes will roll back in terror.
At such a time, the views of a self and a life-essence are extremely difficult to manage;
they are like the great suffering of a turtle that has escaped from its shell.
You, O worthy one, must not take a drowsy understanding and mistake it for the truth.
If you have not yet removed even a hair’s breadth of the covering, do you still understand?
There is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house.
Furthermore, you are not yet one who has attained peace and happiness;
you merely form large groups to interfere with the affairs of others,
like wild deer darting here and there.
You merely know to seek clothing for the sake of food.
If you act like this, how can you be said to practice the Way of the King? Neither kings nor ministers would constrain you;
it was your parents who released you to leave the household life.
Donors from the ten directions provide you with food and clothing,
and the local deities and dragon spirits protect you;
yet you must also possess a sense of shame and gratitude to truly succeed.
Do not let others down.
On the long bed, they sit in rows, their minds dissolving into the ground;
this is what is called peace and happiness.
Up until now, you have merely been sustained by gruel and rice;
you will soon become like a rotting winter melon,
cast away to be buried in the earth.
Karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis to rely upon.
Why, O śramaṇa, have you come to such a state?
It is just like all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth.
I call this the kalpa-abiding of hell.
If you do not realize it now, by tomorrow or the day after,
you will see yourself transformed and entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
They are made to pull plows and drag harrows, with iron bits in their mouths and saddles upon their backs;
they are pounded by pestles and ground in mills, or burned and boiled in water and fire.
To leave this great suffering is not easy.
You will surely experience great fear.
Do you think this is something you have brought upon yourself?
If you had truly understood, from the very beginning across eternal kalpas, I would never have given you this news.
If you do not understand the causes and conditions of these afflictions and evil karmas,
you will not find rest for even one or two kalpas;
you must know that they shall last until you are as long-lived as a vajra.

I wish to establish a temple here to repay my past causes."
When he was clearing the weeds to establish the foundation, auspicious clouds covered the sun,
lingering atop the peak for a long time without dispersing;
consequently, it was named Mount Chongyun (Heavy Clouds).
Previously, the valley abounded with fierce beasts, all of which departed of their own accord.
When the dragon pool was filled to open a path,
the dragon within the pool also moved to another location.
Later, Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang dynasty bestowed upon it the name Changxing.
Disciples gathered there in great numbers.
Once, when the Master ascended the hall, a monk asked:
"What is it like to return to the root and attain the essential meaning?
The Master said,
"It is already forgotten."
A questioner asked, "Unexpectedly, dust has arisen; what is the single path for advancing?
The Master said, "Grass has already grown beneath your feet; ahead lies a pit ten thousand fathoms deep."
Question: "The essential path is level and open; how should one tread upon it?
The Master said:
"If I were to point it out to you, you would go off toward the east, west, south, or north."
Question: "What was it like before the Buddha appeared in the world?
The Master said:
"A heap of mud."
Question: "What is the meaning of 'Zhongyun Cheng'?
The Master said:

Question: What are words that cut through iron?
The Master said:
"Better to die than to transgress."
A question was asked: "What is the realm of Chongyun?
The Master replied: "Flowers do not bloom throughout the four seasons, yet fragrant grasses flourish during the three months of winter.
The Master returned once more to his native mountain, where he founded a monastery and gathered disciples.
Forty-five years passed.
In his leisure time from instructing others, he composed over a thousand verses of praise and eulogy,
and ordained fifteen hundred disciples.
Wang Yanchao, the Regional Inspector of Yongxing,
had long frequented the master’s courtyard and once wished to don the black robes of a monk.
The master stopped him, saying:
"You shall later achieve honor and distinction; it will be sufficient for you to serve as an external protector of the teaching.
Subsequently, things indeed came to pass exactly as the Master had said.
When he met the Master again while stationed at Yongxing, he honored and reverenced him even more.

In the sixth month of summer in the third year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty (the Bingchen year), the Master went to the provincial seat to take leave of the Duke, entrusting him with the affairs of the mountain gate.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, his physical health remained unimpaired.
He offered these instructions to his disciples, presenting them with a verse:
I have a single-room cottage, Built for me by my parents;
I have lived in it for eighty years, But lately I have noticed it is falling into decay.
I had early intended to move my dwelling, but as affairs involve both aversion and affection,
I waited until others had demolished it; thus, with neither side obstructing the other,
I passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was eighty-four years of age and sixty-four years since his ordination;
his stupa was erected at his native mountain.
Chan Master Youzhang of Ruilong Monastery in Hangzhou was the nephew of the Tang Prime Minister Xiahou Zizhi.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, his paternal uncle, the Minister of Works, was stationed as governor in Guangling.
The Master was then seven years old; while visiting Huizhao Temple, he heard the recitation of the Lotus Sutra and resolved to seek ordination.
His paternal uncle initially would not grant permission;
because [the boy] consequently ceased eating and drinking,
his uncle was compelled to consent.
He took Huiyuan as his teacher.
At seventeen, he received full ordination;
at twenty-five, he traveled to various dhyāna assemblies.
Shushan Baishui received the heart-instructions from both masters,
who held him in high esteem.
In the thirteenth year of the Xiantong era, he arrived at Jiangling.
Later, Master Tengteng instructed him, saying, "Go to Tiantai to seek a place of stillness to dwell; when you meet An, stop there.
Furthermore, he encountered Master Hanzhan, who patted him and recorded this: [text omitted].
"Forty years hence, there shall be a Bodhisattva-King from beneath the *jinzi* (turban) mountain who will descend upon the south of the River.
At that time, my Way shall flourish."
The two recluses each bestowed secret instructions upon him.
He soon reached Mount Tiantai and founded Fudang Monastery in Jing’an Township;
thus he realized the meaning of the words "leaping and soaring."
Furthermore, the assembly requested that he reside at Yinyong Monastery.
In the fourth year of the Zhonghe era, when famine and pestilence ravaged the region east of the Zhe River,
the Master [traveled] through the three prefectures of Wenzhou, Taizhou, and Mingzhou.
He collected and buried several thousand remains;
at that time, he was called the Great Being of Increasing Compassion (Beizeng Dashi).
During the Qianning era, Master Xuefeng traveled through the region.
He left behind his master’s *tāla*-leaf whisk and departed.
In the third year of the Tiānyòu era, Qián Shàngfù dispatched the envoy Tóng Jiàn to enter the mountains bearing garments and incense to extend an invitation.
The Master led his disciples to the provincial court,
where he was appointed as the Great Master Zhide and installed in the Hall of Meritorious Ministers.
Emperor Rixin asked the Dharma Master to establish a *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light) ritual site annually on Mount Tiantai.

Great assemblies of both clergy and laity from various commanderies were held there for over a month; this "Great Assembly of Radiance" (*Guangming Dahui*) originated with the Master. As the Master was about to take his leave to return to the mountains, [the Emperor] said:

The King’s devotion increased, and he established Rui’ong Monastery (Rui Longyuan) at the palace grounds; King Wenmu renamed it Baoshan Monastery (Baoshanyuan) and invited [the Master] to propagate the Dharma.
At that time, the Chan school flourished.
This was indeed the fulfillment of that simple, earnest prediction.
The Master ascended the hall and said to the assembly:

"In recent years, I have traveled abroad to the regions beyond the Yangtze River, through Lingnan, Jing, and Hu; wherever there were monasteries of realized masters, I have visited them all to seek instruction."
It is because we have gathered here today with all of you,
each desiring to know the ultimate destination. Yet,
throughout all quarters, there is ultimately no divergent teaching.
Simply instruct the person to bring this frantic mind to rest and cease seeking it elsewhere.
Just follow conditions while abiding in reality, yet there is no reality to be followed;
enjoy things as they arise according to the moment, yet there is no moment that can be employed.
Even if you were to show compassion by speaking with bitter words, you still could not call day night;
yet you are even more skillful than that.
In the end, one can never point east and call it west.
Even if one were able to do so, that would merely be a supernatural manifestation of wonders; it is no concern of mine.
If those who merely parrot words do not examine themselves and recognize their own errors,
they are like those who wish to pluck flowers from the sky or grasp the moon from the waves;
will they ever attain true mental power?
"You all should now each withdraw for a moment and reflect;
if you suddenly agree to go, only then will you know that this old fellow Rui-long had no choice but to take such an excessively circuitous route.
Will you still agree?"
At that time, there was a monk who asked, "What is the realm of Rui Long?
The Master said:
"You say you do not see it; can you not?
He asked, "What is one within the realm?
The Master said:
"The future is to be feared.
[A monk] asked, "When it is vast and empty, without a single cloud, what is the mid-autumn moon?
The Master said:
"It is best when there are no clouds.
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then the single orb hangs high and ten thousand nations behold it together.
The Master said:
It is difficult to speak of the ultimate truth with one who has eyes distorted by pressing upon them.
In the fourth month of summer in the second year of Tiānchéng (the Dinghai year), the Master requested a tomb and stupa;
the Shangfu (Imperial Father) then commissioned Lù Rénzhāng for this task.
He selected a superior site at Xiguan to construct a pagoda and establish a monastery.
An imperial plaque was bestowed to grant it its name, and monks were appointed to guard it;
furthermore, he changed the name of Tiantai Yilong to Yijie.
When the construction of the stupa was completed,
the Master entered the palace courtyard to take leave of the Senior Father (Li Shaoxu),
entrusting him with the matters of protecting the Dharma and showing compassion to the people.
He passed away peacefully according to his predetermined date.
His father-in-law, moved by grief and sorrow, dispatched the Monastic Head to assemble the virtuous elders of the city to welcome him into the stupa.
He was eighty-seven years of age.
At seventy years of age.

Three days later, Touzi asked the administrative officer,

not standing at the gate of the rustic elder."

Facing the eyes, who can depict the radiance of the moon?
In the azure pond, the sun-face and moon-face;
the perfect circle, Mount Sumeru and Mount Sumeru.
A single finger points to the face of the moon;
its subtle radiance shines forth. How could Master Mingzhao say that it violates the directions, for even the dust of the directions is not what the finger points to?

what profound merit is this? Is it so, or is it not?
Chan Master Hui of Huangbo Mountain in Yinzhou was a native of Luoyang. Chan Master Hui of Huangbo Mountain in Yinzhou was a person of Luoyang.
In his youth, he left home to study the sutras and śāstras.

"The Great Being’s restraint of discipline is identical to the śrāvaka precepts I originally received."
These all involve both maintaining and violating the precepts.
However, regarding the increase or decrease of factors within the *pien-chu* (the categories of offenses), the underlying intent behind the general and specific regulations differs.
Since these matters are subtle and difficult to guard against, [one must be diligent].
Furthermore, among the practices for gathering virtue, one has never performed even a small portion;
how much less so regarding the benefit of sentient beings?
Moreover, how can one feel attachment to this worldly body and life, which are as fleeting as bubbles and illusions?
Consequently, he suspended his lecture sessions and intended to cast his body into the water to feed the scaly creatures. Having formed this thought,
he was about to set out.
By chance, two practitioners from the Second Dhyāna Heaven joined him for a cordial conversation,
saying, "There are many wise teachers in the South;
why do you remain stagnant in this single corner?"
The Master then turned his resolve toward traveling to seek out teachers.
As the frontier checkpoints were strictly guarded,
he said to the officials in charge:
"I do not come here to dally with the mountains and waters;
I swear to seek the Way of the Patriarchs.
On another day, I shall surely not forget your kindness."
The guards observed his resolve and consequently did not detain him harshly;
they further said to him, "Since you,
Master, have forgotten your own person for the sake of the Dharma..."
As he was returning, he vowed not to be stingy with what he had heard.
The Master joyfully thanked him and went directly to Shushan.
At that time, Master Ren was seated in the Dharma Hall receiving visitors.
The Master first looked over the assembly and then posed the question:
"What is it like when one departs in a single kṣaṇa?
Shushan replied: "It is completely filled."
"O Empty Space, how will you go?
The Master said,
"It would be better not to go than to fill up empty space."
Shushan then ceased [speaking].
The Master descended from the hall and visited the First Seat.
The First Seat said:
"I have just observed that the words you spoke in response to the Abbot were most extraordinary.
The Master said, "This was merely a spontaneous occurrence; it was truly accidental."
"I venture to hope that you will compassionately instruct this ignorant and deluded one.
The First Seat said,
"In a single kṣaṇa, is there still any room for deliberation?"
Upon hearing these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment;
he prostrated in gratitude and withdrew to the tea hall, where grief and joy mingled within him for three days.
He subsequently resided at Huangbo Mountain, where he gathered a great assembly and expounded the Dharma; the second patriarch passed away at this very mountain.
Today, his entire body remains within the stupa as if alive.

The donkey-faced beast asked,

Chan Master Guiren of Lingquan at Changshui in Luojing.

The Master said:

Chan Master Sheng of Dajian Mountain in Anzhou; the third-generation abbot of Dajian Mountain in Anzhou was asked: "A lost person wandering on the wrong path requests the Master to point directly."

In the winding mountain stream, the water flows slowly.

On Mount Daxiong, a tiger gave birth to a lion cub.

Chan Master Yun of Zhengqin Monastery in Changzhou was a native of Weifu who served as the first abbot of Zhengqin Monastery in Changzhou.
His secular surname was Han.
He left home to become a monk in his youth, yet remained with the youthful complexion of a child even in old age.

The Master said,

He asked, "How does one attain it?
The Master said,

During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, the Master was about to enter parinirvāṇa and announced this in advance to the assembly.
When the appointed time arrived, the men and women of the entire city rushed to the monastery.
Having finished his final instructions,
the Master sat peacefully and passed away.
His disciples buried him behind the monastery.

it remained solemn and majestic, with both hair and fingernails having grown long.
He then performed the cremation ceremony to the east of the city.
The true bone relics were collected and the stupa was rebuilt.

[the Master replied: "It is like a person who has lost their way."

The Monk of the Three Phases of Jingzhao—Monk of the Three Phases of Jingzhao."
Question: "What is the seamless stupa?
The Master said:

He asked, "What is it like to be the person within the stupa?

Chan Master Shanjing of Yong’an Temple in Jingzhao, Dharma heir of Chan Master Yuan’an of Qianlepu: Chan Master Shanjing of Yong’an Temple in Jingzhao was a native of Jingzhao.
Her surname was Wang.
Her father served as a regional governor.
Her mother became pregnant after dreaming of a golden image.
The Master studied Confucian learning from his youth and became widely versed in various doctrines.
At the age of twenty-seven, he suddenly grew weary of worldly illusions;
he went secretly to Mount Zhongnan to pay homage to Chan Master Guangdu, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
In the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, he went south to pay his respects to Chan Master Le Pu’an.
The Master esteemed him and permitted him to enter the inner quarters;
he subsequently oversaw the garden duties and diligently managed the affairs of the community.
A monk took his leave of Yuepu.
Yuepu said, "The mountains surround you on all four sides; where will you go, Ācārya?"
The monk had no reply.
Yuepu said, "I grant you ten days to provide a response that hits the mark; if you succeed, I shall let you depart."
The monk searched in secret for a long time without saying a word.
While walking about, he happened to enter the garden.
The Master asked him in surprise: "Why have you been silent?"
"Venerable Elder, did you not take your leave?
Why are you here now?
The monk explained the reason in full and earnestly requested that he speak on his behalf.
The Master, having no choice, spoke on his behalf:
"How can dense bamboo obstruct the flow of water?
How can high mountains hinder the flight of wild clouds?"
The monk leaped for joy, and the Master instructed him, saying:
"When responding to the Upādhyāya,
you need not speak of this as being 'good' or 'tranquil' speech."
The monk then informed Le Pu.
Le Pu asked, "Who uttered these words?"
He said, "So-and-so. Le Pu replied,
"Those are not your words."
The monk related in detail what the head gardener had instructed him.
That evening, when Le Pu ascended the hall, he said to the assembly,
"Do not underestimate the head gardener."
On another day, while he was residing at a city altar (chénghuáng), five hundred people constantly followed him.
The Master then took his leave of Lèpǔ and returned north to his former mountain, where he built a thatched hut and settled there.
Monastics and laypeople alike turned toward him for refuge.
He traveled again to Mount Emei and subsequently resided at Xingyuan,
where the regional commander, Duke Wang, treated him with profound respect.
Later, upon returning to his native village, he found that the old temple had fallen into ruin following the ravages of war.
A regional military commander established the Yong’an Chan Monastery for him to reside in,
where more than five hundred disciples gathered.
A monk asked,

Chan Master Guichen of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou: Chan Master Guichen of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou was a native of Changshan.
His secular surname was Li.
When he was a child, he ate only vegetarian food once a day and his speech was extraordinary.
Upon reaching adulthood, he took leave of his parents and entered the service of Great Master Wuxiang at Wansui Temple in the local prefecture.
Having cast off his robes and ascended to the precepts, he studied the Vinaya.

Thereupon, he sought out the Southern School.
He first visited Yunju and Xuefeng, attending to them with diligent devotion;

Later, he met the Great Master Xuansha Zongyi.
A single word from him awakened him, leaving his mind vast and free of delusion.
Xuansha once asked him:
"The three realms are mind-only; how do you understand this?
The Master pointed to his leaning staff and asked, "What does the Abbot call this?"
Xuansha said, "Rely on yourself. [The monk] said,
"Master, you do not understand that the triple world is mind-only."
Xuansha said, "I call this 'bamboo and wood';
what do you call it?"
Guichen also called it "bamboo and wood. Xuansha said,
