This refers to the Tenth Patriarch, Chan Master Xingsi. He was the Dharma heir of National Teacher Deshao of Mount Tiantai. [He was] the Dharma heir of National Teacher Deshao of Mount Tiantai: Chan Master Yanshou of Yongming Temple in Hangzhou, also known as Chan Master Zhijue of Huiriji Yongming Temple in Hangzhou. Yanshou.
He was a native of Yuhang and surnamed Wang.
From his childhood, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-vehicle.
Having undergone the capping ceremony,
he abstained from pungent foods; he ate only one meal a day and recited the Lotus Sutra with seven lines at a time.
By the time he reached sixty, he was able to recite them all from memory.
He moved a flock of sheep to kneel and listen.
At the age of twenty-eight, he served as the military commander of Huating.
When Master Yongming of Cuiyan moved his residence to Longce Temple and extensively propagated the profound teachings,
King Wenmu of Wuyue, recognizing the Master’s aspiration for the Way,
fulfilled his wish by granting him permission to leave the household life.
He took Cuiyan as his teacher.
He performed manual labor to provide for the assembly, completely forgetting his own person;
he wore no silk or flossed cotton, and his food lacked rich flavors.
He sustained himself with wild vegetables and coarse cloth tunics to pass the days and nights.
He then traveled to Mount Tiantai, where he practiced meditative concentration for ninety days on the summit of Mount Tianzhu;
there, a bird resembling a *chican* (a small shorebird) built its nest within the folds of his robes.
When he went to pay his respects to National Teacher Yao, he was immediately recognized by the Master as one of great potential; Yao secretly transmitted the profound essence of the teachings to him.
He then said to the Master, "You have a karmic affinity with the Yuan-shuai."
On another day, he secretly received a prediction of his future enlightenment regarding the great flourishing of Buddhist affairs.

Initially residing at Xuedou Mountain in Mingzhou, students gathered there in great numbers. In the first year of the Chanding era (998 CE), the imperial title "Zisheng Temple" was bestowed upon it. The Master ascended the hall and said:
At Xuedou, here, a torrent of a thousand fathoms flows without ceasing for even a moment;
with its wondrous cliffs of ten thousand cubits, there is no place to set foot. Where, then, do you all take a step forward?
At that time, a monk asked,
"How does one tread upon the single path of Xuedou?
The Master said:
At every step, cold blossoms gather; in every word, one reaches the bottom of the ice.
In the first year of the Jianlong era, King Zhongyi invited him to reside at the new temple on Mount Lingyin as its first patriarch.
The following year, he was again invited to reside at the Great Monastery of Yongming as its second patriarch.
The assembly numbered over two thousand.
A monk asked:
"What is the wondrous purport of Yongming?
The Master said,
"Add more incense."
He said, "I thank you for your instruction.
The Master said, "Be glad; do not involve yourself in it."
The Master had a verse that said:
If you wish to know the essential meaning of Yongming, Look at the lake before the gate:
When the sun shines, radiance arises; When the wind comes, waves are stirred.
A student asked, "I have been at Yongming for a long time;
why is it that I do not understand the house style of Yongming?
The Master said:
He said, "I do not understand how to grasp it at the point where there is no understanding. The Master said: "How can you understand at the point where there is no understanding?"
A calf born from an ox’s womb; red dust rising from the blue sea.

even within the cycle of the six realms of rebirth, one cannot escape.

What, then, is this sutra?
The Master said:
"For a long time it has turned without ceasing; it is neither meaning nor sound.
[The student] asked: "How then should one receive and uphold it?"
The Master said,
"If you wish to receive and uphold [this teaching], you must listen with your eyes.
He asked, "What is the Great Perfect Mirror?"
The Master said,
"A broken sand pot.
The Master resided at the Yongming Monastery for fifteen years.
He ordained one thousand seven hundred disciples.
In the seventh year of the Kaibao era, he entered Mount Tiantai and conferred the full precepts upon approximately ten thousand people.
He constantly administered the Bodhisattva precepts to the sevenfold assembly.
At night, he offered food to the spirits and deities;
at dawn, he released various living beings beyond counting;
and throughout the six periods of the day, he scattered flowers.
With the remaining strength from his practice of the Way, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* thirteen thousand times.
He composed the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles,
and his poems, verses, and rhapsodies totaled several million words.
It was disseminated beyond the seas.
King Gao-li, having perused the Master’s teachings,
dispatched an envoy bearing a letter to express the etiquette of a disciple.
He was presented with a *kāṣāya* woven from gold thread, a rosary of purple crystal, a golden water pitcher, and other items.
Thirty-six monks from that country personally received his seal of transmission;
they subsequently returned to their own land and each transformed one region.
In the twelfth month of the year Yihai, the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he manifested illness.
On the twenty-sixth day at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he burned incense, addressed the assembly, and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
On the sixth day of the first month of the following year, he was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Daci.
He was seventy-two years of age and forty-two years since his ordination.
Emperor Taizong bestowed upon him the name Shouning Chan Monastery.

Regarding the four lands:
first is the land of the eternally quiescent light, the dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), wherein the Dharma-body resides;
here, the body and the land correspond to one another. Second is the land of true recompense without obstruction, which subsumes the two types of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
The land of self-enjoyment is where the Reward Buddha himself resides.

The land of other-enjoyment is where Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages reside. The three types of lands characterized by a remainder of expedient means, as well as the fourth type—the land of shared purity and impurity—are all lands of transformation for the sake of responding to beings.
In reality, the abodes of bodhisattvas prior to the stages, of those of the two vehicles, and of ordinary beings are neither bodies nor lands; they possess neither superiority nor inferiority.
It is only for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings that bodies and lands are provisionally described and distinguished as superior or inferior.
Because the Master had attained the mutual fusion of body and land and the non-obstruction of the provisional and the real,
he expounded [the teachings] day and night for over thirty years,
producing four kinds of benefit and possessing the four *siddhāntas*— that is, they were all-pervasive.
*Dāna* is translated as "giving" (*śī*).
The Dharma of the Chan Master was bestowed universally upon sentient beings, benefiting them according to their faculties like a cloud;
through the *loka-siddhānta*, he produced the benefit of joy, and so forth. His disciple Guanding recorded ten thousand words daily and compiled them into this work.
Collectively, these are categorized as the Tiantai Teachings;
specifically, they are divided into various sections and genres.

These include the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), the *Dazhi* and *Xiaozhi* (Greater and Lesser Calming and Contemplation), the *Jinguangming*, *Renwang*, *Weimo* (Vimalakīrti), and *Niepan* (Nirvāṇa) sutras, the *Zhiguan Zhang* (Chapters on Stopping and Contemplation), the *Shiwanjing* (Contemplation of the Sixteen Visualizations), and so forth, along with the *Sijiao Chanmen* (The Dhyāna Gate of the Four Teachings). In total, there are over one hundred fascicles, which have been transmitted through successive generations and flourished in the regions of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Deluded and foolish people do not understand that Buddha-nature is true and spontaneous,
and neither has it causes and conditions nor does it require cultivation or construction.
Failing to recognize that the three poisons are illusory,
one falsely clings to the cycles of birth, aging,
and death. It is never too late to turn back from the days of former delusion.
Today, for the first time, I realize it is not early.
Holding and violating are non-dual; when a man of such realization functions without obstruction, he is no longer constrained by the precepts and rules.
The observance and violation of precepts are fundamentally unborn; fools are bound by them,
while for the wise, all conditioned actions are empty.
The Śrāvakas encounter obstacles wherever they turn;
the Great Being’s physical eyes possess perfect penetration,
whereas the divine eyes of the Two Vehicles are obscured by cataracts.
They falsely cling to existence and non-existence within the void,
failing to realize that form and mind are unimpeded;
thus, the Bodhisattva dwells together with worldly beings.
The pure has never been defiled by the world;
fools crave attachment to nirvana,
while the wise [find it] in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of birth-and-death.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty and beyond verbal expression.
This verse was composed as a brief summary of dependent origination for the sake of the "Son of Man" (manuṣya-putra).
Even a child of one hundred years who lacks wisdom [would understand it].
A child may possess wisdom equal to that of a hundred-year-old.
The Buddha and sentient beings are not two; the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual. Sentient beings and the Buddha are no different.
Great wisdom is not distinct from folly.
Why seek jewels elsewhere? Within the field of one's own body, there is naturally a bright pearl.
The right path and the deviant path are non-dual.
One thoroughly understands that ordinary beings and sages share the same path;
that delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction;
and that nirvana and birth-and-death are one and the same.
Ultimately, they take emptiness and stillness as their object of focus;
they seek only the purity and vacuity of mental conceptions,
such that not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Tranquil and spontaneous, one enters the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa*.
Phenomena and principle are non-dual; in this non-duality of phenomena and principle, the sovereign mind-king is tranquil and free.
In the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the ten entanglements (*daśasaṃyojana*) are originally non-existent.
All things are nothing other than the work of the Buddha;
why, then, must one restrain the mind and practice seated meditation?
Delusive thoughts are originally empty and quiescent.
There is no need to sever攀緣 (pān-yuan, objects of attachment).
For the wise, there is no mind to be found;
naturally, there is neither contention nor clamor.
Failing to recognize the unconditioned Great Way,
when will one realize its profound mystery?
Buddhas and sentient beings are of one kind.
Sentient beings are themselves the World-Honored One;
yet ordinary people give rise to false discrimination,
clinging to existence within non-existence and wandering in delusion.
Having thoroughly realized that greed and anger are empty and quiescent, where is there that is not the gate of truth?
Stillness and turbulence are non-dual; stillness and turbulence are non-dual. Śrāvakas loathe clamor and seek stillness.
It is like discarding flour while seeking cakes;
the cake has always been nothing other than flour,
though its manifestations follow the person through a hundred transformations.
Afflictions are themselves awakening;
the absence of mind is itself the absence of objects;
birth and death are no different from nirvana.
Greed and hatred are like flames and shadows;
the wise have no mind to seek a Buddha,
while the foolish cling to what is false and what is true.
One's life will pass in vain and toil;
one shall not behold the Tathāgata’s wondrous crown,
nor realize that the nature of lust is empty.
The boiling cauldrons and glowing coals cool of their own accord.
Good and evil are not two; good and evil are not two, and my own body and mind are joyful.
Transcendentally, there is neither good nor evil.
The Dharmakāya is sovereign and without fixed location; everything encountered by the eye is none other than perfect enlightenment.
The six sense objects are originally empty and quiescent, yet ordinary beings delusively give rise to attachment.
Nirvana and birth-and-death are equal;
throughout the four seas, who is favored or slighted?
The unconditioned Great Way is spontaneous.
Do not employ the mind to calculate or speculate.
The Bodhisattva is carefree yet spiritually penetrating;
whatever they do always contains wondrous awakening.
The śrāvakas cling to the dharma as they sit in meditation,
binding themselves like silkworms spinning their own cocoons;
yet the nature of dharmas is from the beginning perfectly luminous.
Once the illness has been cured, what need is there to cling to the medicine?
Having fully realized the equality of all phenomena,
one dwells in a state of serene, pure, and joyful emptiness.
Form and emptiness are non-dual; in the dharma-nature of form and emptiness, there is fundamentally no blue or yellow.
Sentient beings vainly compose literary works, and I and others speak of "this" and "that," of shamatha and vipaśyanā.
My own mind is restless and deranged;

When shall I realize the true and eternal?
Unable to treat one's own illness,
one instead instructs others on medicinal formulas;
outwardly, this appears to be virtuous.
Within the mind, one is like a jackal or a wolf;
the fool fears hell, while the wise person views it no differently than heaven.
The mind never arises toward objects;
every step taken is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual.
Sentient beings themselves create their own divisions;
if they wish to eliminate the three poisons,
yet remain far removed from them, they will not escape calamity and misfortune.
The wise know that the mind is Buddha;
the ignorant delight in going to the West.
Birth and death are non-dual; birth and death are non-dual; all worldly phenomena are like illusions.
Birth and death are like thunder and lightning;
the Dharmakāya is sovereign and perfectly penetrating,
entering and exiting mountains and rivers without obstruction.
Inverted delusions are fundamentally empty;
Prajñā is without confusion or disorder;
the three poisons are inherently liberated.
What need is there to collect the mind through meditative contemplation?
It is simply because fools do not understand;
they merely follow the determinations of the precepts.
Failing to recognize the true suchness of quiescence,
when will one attain the other shore?
For the wise, there is no evil to be severed.
The application of mental activity follows the principles of convergence and dispersal;
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is originally empty and quiescent,
and is not fettered by birth and death.
If one wishes to sever and eliminate afflictions,
such a person is an ignorant fool;
for afflictions are themselves bodhi.
What need is there to seek dhyāna and contemplation separately?
In the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), there is neither Buddha nor Māra;
the essence of mind is formless and without parts.
Having severed non-duality and severed non-duality, the Great Man acts with majestic dignity;

Firm and stable as a vajra,

it is serene, being neither annihilated nor eternal.
The greed and anger for the five desires are the Buddha;
hell is no different from heaven.
Only fools give rise to false discrimination.
Wandering through birth and death in wild abandon,
the wise realize that form is without obstruction,
while the śrāvakas are all filled with distress.

They merely pursue words and phrases;
yet words and phrases are not the true Path.

In the mind there are vipers, snakes, and scorpions;
as soon as one is stung by them, one suffers injury.
One does not understand how to extract the meaning from within the words.
When shall we ever reunite with the True and Eternal?
Having died, one enters the Avīci Hell,
where the consciousness suffers calamity and misfortune in vain.
The Dharma Master’s teaching on the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional is excellent;

and he employs written words to transform others.
This only serves to further increase the birth and old age of others;
truth and falsehood are fundamentally non-dual.

The fourfold assembly gathered like clouds to listen to the lectures;
the discourse on the high seat was grand and expansive,
with those from the south and north seats vying with one another.

yet not relinquishing the three poisons within the mind—

yet the nature of that precept is like space,
abiding neither within nor without this Sahā world.

A Verse on Clarifying the Way by Venerable Guichen of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou. One verse on clarifying the Way by Venerable Guichen of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou: The ultimate Way is profound and vast; it cannot be proclaimed through words.
Words proclaim it, yet they do not point to it; who could say that it exists?
It pervades every place—how could it be compared to the true or the void?
Even if one were to distinguish between the true and the void, it would be like a reflection appearing in a mirror.
Although existence and non-existence manifest, they do not cause harm anywhere.
Since there is no harm and no location, what can restrict or obstruct?
Without relying on the achievement of effort, how could it be otherwise by nature?
It is the natural law that both [the speaker and the listener] are like lips and teeth;
if one presents this [teaching] in such a way as to bury the essential tenets,
those tenets— which are not presented for the sake of personal opinion— cannot be seen or heard.
Seeing and hearing are not liberated, like the moon reflected in water;
failing to understand this is, conversely, an extraneous dharma.
A single dharma has a form that obscures your eyes.
The eyes do not see clearly while the world remains steep and treacherous.
My school is extraordinary and magnificent, manifesting its brilliance right before one's face.
Both Buddhas and sentient beings alike receive the power of this grace.
It is not found by bowing the head in deliberation; it is difficult to attain.
It breaks through the gateway of the face, covering heaven and earth.
You must quickly realize it and cast off the root-dusts.
Since you do not understand, let me speak now in jest.

the original nature of sentient beings is fundamentally unstained.

Realize that this illusory nature is identical to a mirage.

The Eight Verses on the Graded Stages by Bai Juyi, with Preface Preface: In the eighth month of autumn, the nineteenth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a Great Master named Master Ning.
He passed away at the Bowl-Stupa Courtyard of Shengshan Temple in the Eastern Capital.
In the second month of the spring of the following year, the traveler from the East, Bai Juyi,
composed the "Verses on the Eight Gradual Stages."
The verse consists of six lines,
each line being four characters in praise.
Initially, when I lived in seclusion, I once sought the essential meaning of the mind from the Master.
The Master bestowed these words upon me:
"Contemplation" and "Awakening."
They are called concentration, wisdom, and clarity.
It is called penetration,
it is called deliverance,
and it is called relinquishment.
Thus, it entered his ears and pierced his heart.
Alas! While the Master’s reward-body (vipākakāya) has now passed away, the Master’s eight words shall never pass away.
How sublime! These eight words are indeed the gradual gateway to the contemplation of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, from self-contemplation to relinquishment, they are praised in successive order.
He expanded a single word into a verse,
which is called the "Eight Verses on the Gradual Path.
This was intended to elucidate the mind-teachings of his Master.
Furthermore, Mingju dares not let these [rites] fall into ruin.

kneeling, he wailed aloud and then departed.
The verse says:
Contemplating with the eye of the mind, one observes the external signs within the mind;
from what do they arise, and from what are they lost?
Observing again and again, one distinguishes the real from the false;
though awakening perceives only the real, it is constantly obscured by the false.
Once the real and the false are distinguished, awakening arises from within them.
Without departing from delusive existence, one attains true emptiness.
When true suchness is firmly established and does not cease,
delusion will not arise.
The source of the six sense faculties is as profoundly still as calm water;
this is what is called meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).
Thus one is liberated from birth and death.
Wisdom is concentrated through meditative absorption;
yet even meditative absorption still possesses attachments.
Sustain this with wisdom;
when there is wisdom, there is no obstruction,
like a pearl upon a tray.
The wisdom of the settled pearl is luminous;
luminosity and concentration are in harmony.
It is through their union that there is luminosity.
It illuminates all myriad things;
no object can conceal its form,
just like a great round mirror.
There is that which responds and that which is insentient.
When both penetration and wisdom reach their ultimate, clarity arises;
where there is clarity, there is no obscurity.
When clarity reaches its ultimate point, there is penetration; when there is penetration, there is no obstruction.
What is meant by "no obstruction"?
Their transformations are sovereign;
their collective powers are not constant,
but change in accordance with thought.
The manifested forms do not truly exist;
they appear according to one's aspirations.
This is great compassion.
To save ten thousand by means of one:
once the myriad sufferings have been relinquished and all beings have been delivered,
even great compassion is relinquished.
Since suffering is not real,
compassion is likewise provisional.
Therefore, sentient beings—
"Truly there is no one who delivers.

like the bright moon in a crystalline sky;
as its reflection turns, the functioning of the mind ceases.

thus, one earnestly points to the moon.

do not lose your way regarding the needle that pierces through water.

the stone horse returning from its journey emerges from the sand-cage.

Quiescence and non-action are called the principle-entry (*li-ru*).
As for the practice-entry (*xing-ru*),

All other practices are entirely included within these.
What are the four? First, the practice of requiting grievances.
Second, practice in accordance with conditions;
third, practice free from seeking;
fourth, practice in conformity with the Dharma.
What is the practice of requiting grievances?
It means that when a practitioner on the path experiences suffering, they should reflect to themselves:
"Throughout countless kalpas in the past, I have abandoned the root for the branches and wandered through the various realms of existence."
I have frequently given rise to resentment and hostility, causing limitless harm.
Although I have committed no offense now, this is the ripening of the fruit of my past misdeeds and evil karma;
it is not something that gods or humans can grant or withhold.
One accepts it with a willing heart and endures it without any grievance or complaint.
As the Sūtra says:
"When encountering suffering, one does not grieve."
Why is this? Because consciousness penetrates;
when this mind arises, it accords with principle.
Because one advances on the Path by embodying resentment toward those who wrong one, it is called the practice of repaying resentment.
Second is the practice of following conditions:
sentient beings lack a self and are all turned by the power of karma and conditions.
Suffering and pleasure are experienced equally, all arising from conditions.
If one obtains superior retributions such as honor and renown,
these are now attained precisely because they were induced by past causes from former lives.
When conditions are exhausted and one returns to non-existence, what joy can there be? Gain and loss follow conditions; the mind neither increases nor decreases.
Unmoved by the wind of joy, one silently accords with the Way.
Therefore, it is said: "Acting in accordance with conditions."
Third, regarding the practitioner who seeks nothing:
worldly people are long deluded and greedily attached everywhere;
this is what is called "seeking."
The wise realize the ultimate truth and turn back from the mundane;
they settle their minds in non-action while their forms follow the turning of conditions.
All phenomena are thus empty, and there is nothing to be desired or delighted in.
Merit and darkness constantly follow one another.
Dwelling long in the three realms is like being in a house on fire;

Because one thoroughly understands this state, one abandons all forms of existence (*bhava*), ceases conceptualization, and is free from seeking.
As the Sūtra says:
"All seeking is suffering; the absence of seeking is bliss."
Having discerned that there is nothing to be sought and taking the realization of this as the practice of the Way,
it is therefore called "the practice of seeking nothing. Fourth is the practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusāri-pratipatti*).
